articles.title: Grammys CEO “Saddened” Over BTS Decision to Not Submit for Awards
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All July 29, 2026 6:12pm Jungkook, V, Jin, RM, Suga, Jimin and J-Hope of BTS speak onstage during the 52nd American Music Awards at MGM Grand Garden Arena on May 25, 2026, in Las Vegas, Nevada. Ethan Miller/Getty Images Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. has issued a lengthy response after BTS announced they wouldn’t be submitting their music for Grammy consideration this year, giving his support to the group over their decision while also addressing critique toward the organization’s newly-created best Asian pop music performance category. “I am saddened to hear that BTS has chosen not to participate in the Grammy Awards process this year, but as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision,” Mason Jr. wrote. “I do want to clarify something that seems to be getting lost in the conversation. The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists.” Related Stories Music White House Claps Back at Noah Kahan for Criticizing Trump's Use of His Song Music BTS Will Not Be Submitting to 2027 Grammy Awards BTS first announced their decision on Tuesday night, sharing posts on Instagram where they said they “hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.” The move came just over a month after the Recording Academy first introduced its new Asian pop category, which, per the Academy, “recognizes artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets, including but not limited to K-pop, J-pop and C-pop, with meaningful use of one or more Asian languages. Awards are presented to the performing artist(s).” The award had received a mixed response from fans, with some arguing the award could keep Asian acts from getting properly recognized in the general categories. In his statement, Mason Jr. said the genre categories don’t”exclude an artist from also submitting and being considered in the General Field.” “Recognition in a genre category and recognition in the General Field are not mutually exclusive,” Mason Jr. said. “An artist can absolutely pursue both.” Mason Jr. further wrote that the Academy adds new categories “never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters.” “The Grammy organization is here to serve music and all the people who make it,” Mason Jr. wrote. “As we continue to expand the reach, our membership and our awards, regardless of geography or language, I want to emphasize that we will continue to listen to the global music community and work to honor and celebrate all the artists whose music moves the world.” BTS isn’t the first act to rebuke the Grammys, as other major stars including The Weeknd, Drake and Morgan Wallen have all decided in recent years not to have their music considered as well. Read Mason Jr.’s full statement below: I am saddened to hear that BTS has chosen not to participate in the Grammy Awards process this year, but as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision. I do want to clarify something that seems to be getting lost in the conversation. The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists. More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized. It’s never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters. I also want to be very clear: submitting music in a genre category such as Asian Pop, or Jazz or Country does not exclude an artist from also submitting and being considered in the General Field categories, including Record of the Year, Album of the Year and Song of the Year. Those categories remain open to any eligible recording, regardless of genre. Recognition in a genre category and recognition in the General Field are not mutually exclusive. An artist can absolutely pursue both. The Grammy organization is here to serve music and all the people who make it. As we continue to expand the reach, our membership and our awards, regardless of geography or language, I want to emphasize that we will continue to listen to the global music community and work to honor and celebrate all the artists whose music moves the world.” THR

articles.title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Aims to Make Box Office History as It Targets High-Flying Opening
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All July 29, 2026 7:29pm MJ (Zendaya) watches Spider-Man work in 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day.' Jay Maidment/Sony Pictures Logo text Spider-Man : Brand New Day looks to close out the month with a big swing, as Sony Pictures ‘ latest superhero feature with Tom Holland and Zendaya eyes an astronomical opening weekend at the box office . After Universal’s The Odyssey enjoyed quite the successful box office journey without major new competition for the past two weeks, Peter Parker and his pals are poised to land the year’s biggest debut and potentially one of the top-grossing openings ever. The studio is projecting a domestic opening of $195 million from 4,300 North American theaters, which is also in line with third-party tracking services. Related Stories Movies Joyce Carol Oates Defends 'Odyssey' Against Translator's Viral Slam: "Crude Language of MAGA Folks" Movies 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings to China's Biggest Superhero Opening in Seven Years This would top last month’s launch for Disney ‘s Toy Story 5 , which opened to $159.6 million domestically, to make Spider-Man: Brand New Day the biggest debut of 2026. This would also put it in the top 10 for domestic opening weekends, beating 2019’s photorealistic The Lion King remake, which holds the No. 10 launch at $191.7 million. The last time a title opened above $200 million domestically was two years ago with Deadpool & Wolverine at $211.4 million. (The record goes to Avengers: Endgame’ s wild 2019 opening of $357.1 million.) Sony projects Spider-Man: Brand New Day to add $270 million from international markets for a global start of $465 million, including a strong showing in China . This would give it the studio’s second-best launch behind Spider-Man: No Way Home ‘ s heroic opening of $600.5 million in 2021, and it would best Spider-Man 3′ s $381.6 million start from 2007. Spider-Man and The Punisher ( Jon Bernthal ) in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Jay Maidment/Sony Pictures Exhibitors are certainly clamoring to show director Destin Daniel Cretton ‘s new Spider-Man film, which centers on the title hero living a lonely existence without his loved ones before a dangerous new foe targets him. Hailing from Sony and Marvel Studios , Brand New Day accounts for 49 percent of this weekend’s showtimes as of Wednesday, according to the Boxoffice Company, as opposed to the 22 percent that The Odyssey held when it opened two weekends ago to $124.5 million domestically for the third-biggest 2026 launch to date. Word of mouth could push the Brand New Day opening much higher, as the film is already off to a flying start with critics. Also starring Sadie Sink , Jacob Batalon , Jon Bernthal and Mark Ruffalo , it holds a 91 percent approval rating from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes. That puts it within similar range of the franchise’s other recent offerings, including 2018’s animated Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse at 97 percent and Spider-Man: No Way Home at 93 percent. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , chief film critic David Rooney writes that Brand New Da y “foregrounds the humanity that has always been Spidey’s greatest strength,” and he praises “a never-better Tom Holland.” Indeed, some analysts are predicting that the buzz around the release will carry Spider-Man: Brand New Day far beyond $195 million. It remains to be seen whether the $260.1 million domestic opening sum for No Way Home , the previous live-action Spider-Man release, could potentially be within reach. Granted, that one had the benefit of the buzz surrounding the return of past Peter Parkers in Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield, not to mention that the release faced no real competition and marked the first post-COVID theatrical visit for many moviegoers who were starved for entertainment experiences. Notably, there has been recent debate about audiences tiring of franchise offerings, given the underperformance of titles from both the superhero variety ( June’s Supergirl ) and otherwise ( May’s The Mandalorian and Grogu ). And yet, this weekend is poised to prove that the filmmaking teams have done an admirable job of handling Marvel Comics’ crown-jewel hero. As Fandango director of analytics and Box Office Theory founder Shawn Robbins tells THR , “Tom Holland, Sony and Marvel Studios’ run of films has remained remarkably fresh, thanks to thoughtful timing and stories that continue to connect with audiences in both new and familiar ways.” He adds, “They’ve consistently met — and often exceeded — expectations, anchored by the kind of character-driven storytelling and big-screen spectacle audiences want from Spider-Man. It’s as much a gold standard as any for how to keep a massively popular character relevant and endearing to multiple generations of moviegoers.” As for Holland, whose first leading role as the character came with 2017’s Spider-Man: Homecoming , it appears likely that Sony will have more chances to continue its winning streak. “It has been the gift of my life,” the actor — who also appears in The Odyssey — told THR at the Brand New Day premiere in Los Angeles about playing Spidey. “I will do it for as long as they’ll have me. So if this movie does good, I guess we’ll see!” Yes, we will. THR

articles.title: Homer Gere Says It’s “Really Funny” Working With Kaia Gerber on ‘The Shards,’ 30 Years After Famous Parents’ Divorce
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All July 29, 2026 8:56pm Kaia Gerber and Homer Gere at 'The Shards' NYC premiere, and Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere in 1993. Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images; Brenda Chase/Online USA, Inc. Logo text It was “really funny” for Homer Gere and Kaia Gerber to be working together on The Shards following their parents’ romantic history. While chatting with E! News at the New York City premiere of Ryan Murphy ‘s new FX series, both actors opened up about their experience sharing the screen 30 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere divorced in 1995. Crawford later remarried Rande Gerber in 1998 and they welcomed Kaia in 2001, while Richard Gere and Carey Lowell got married in 2002, two years after Homer was born. The latter couple ultimately divorced in 2016 and Richard has since tied the knot again with Alejandra Silva. Related Stories TV 'The Shards' Team Details Author Bret Easton Ellis' "Hands-Off Approach" to TV Adaptation, How Series "Incites the Same Feeling" as the Book TV Ryan Murphy Reveals 'American Horror Story' Season 13 Brings Together All Previous Seasons: "It's Like the Avengers" Homer told E! that it was “really funny” to jump into The Shards with Kaia as they “hadn’t met before shooting.” He added, “Two weeks before we met at a bar with all the other cast and we became friends. From the inside, it’s really normal.” “We just became friends as coworkers before we started working, and she’s become a really close friend. It’s been lovely working with her,” the Euphoria actor continued. Kaia echoed a similar sentiment on the red carpet, saying she had “never met Homer until we started filming,” despite both their parents still working in the entertainment industry throughout the last three decades. “It was so lovely to work with him,” the Palm Royale actress added. “He’s so wonderful. He’s so funny. He makes me laugh so hard and he’s the greatest scene partner ever. And really it’s just such a supportive environment and we’ve gotten so close over this process.” The Shards , adapted from Bret Easton Ellis’ book of the same name, follows a group of privileged high school friends as a serial killer strikes across Los Angeles in 1981. Elsewhere on the red carpet, Kaia spoke with The Hollywood Reporter about her reaction to when she first learned Murphy would be adapting Ellis’ novel for the small screen. “I’m a huge Bret Easton Ellis fan and when this book came out, I read it immediately and read it over and over again,” she said. “Then when I heard Ryan was doing it, I’m also the biggest fan of Ryan. He gave me my first ever job. When he told me he got the rights to it , I just got chills and teared up.” The series premieres Aug. 5 on FX. THR

articles.title: ‘The Bombing of Pan Am 103’ Review: Netflix’s Sensitive Lockerbie Drama Is Restrained to a Fault
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All July 30, 2026 12:00am Connor Swindells in 'The Bombing of Pan Am 103.' Courtesy of Netflix “If the word Lockerbie will be associated with this terrible tragedy,” intones a priest at a memorial ceremony, “perhaps it will also be spoken of in the future with admiration through the example of its people.” And so it is in The Bombing of Pan Am 103 , Netflix’s new chronicle of the 1988 attack that claimed 270 lives. It is the people of this small Scottish town, Jonathan Lee’s drama makes clear, who rushed to one another’s aid in the crisis, who worked tirelessly to pursue answers, who embraced mourners from around the world. As a tribute to their compassion and tenacity in the face of horror, the six-part miniseries is above reproach — respectful and respectable, laudatory but dignified. Related Stories Lifestyle Odessa A'Zion and Connor Swindells Honored by Chopard in Cannes: "Really Weird, Crazy and Surreal" Lifestyle Chopard Gala to Host Godmother Isabelle Huppert and Honorees Odessa A'zion and Connor Swindells The Bombing of Pan Am 103 The Bottom Line Respectable but not memorable. Airdate: Thursday, July 30 (Netflix) Cast: Connor Swindells, Patrick J. Adams, Merritt Wever, Peter Mullan, Eddie Marsan, Tony Curran, Phyllis Logan, James Harkness, Nicholas Gleaves, Molly Geddes Creator: Jonathan Lee As a story trying to stand its own test of time, however, the series leaves something to be desired. Better equipped to pore over the past than reflect on its enduring significance, The Bombing of Pan Am 103 , starring Connor Swindells and Patrick J. Adams , delivers a less-than-memorable portrait of an indelible event. To recap, for those who do not recall the original events (or, for that matter, the 2025 series Lockerbie: A Search for Truth ): On the night of Dec. 21, a commercial plane en route from London to New York exploded about 60 miles outside Glasgow, killing everyone on board plus several more on the ground. If what exactly had transpired was not immediately obvious — it takes the better part of the Michael Keillor-directed premiere for law enforcement and intelligence agencies to determine it was a bombing at all, and then four of the next five hours to figure out who was behind it — the magnitude of the destruction is. The physical debris was scattered over a massive area of roughly 800 square miles. The emotional and political wreckage was spread further still, with victims from 21 countries (including 179 from the U.S., spurring the involvement of the FBI), hundreds of bereaved and countless witnesses, detectives, lawyers and more involved in the aftermath. With a scope so unwieldy, Lee does what he can to keep his drama efficient, sensitive, human-scaled. From that vast population of people directly affected by the incident, he trains his attention on a few key figures, including a dogged Scottish police officer, Ed McCusker (Swindells), and a slippery FBI agent, Dick Marquise (Adams). In relaying the unimaginable destruction of the event, Lee eschews sensationalism for sobriety. Graphic violence or gore are nowhere to be seen, and even the crash itself is depicted through the horror of Lockerbie residents stumbling outside to find their world transformed into rubble and hellfire, rather than through the terror experienced by those on the plane. At its best, this restraint dovetails with the story unfolding before us. The Scottish and American teams piece together their theory painstakingly over time, poring over clues as small as a torn clothing label and negotiating every single disclosure with their counterparts across borders. Similarly, Lee assembles his story via small but striking details: the eerie orange of a burning sky at night, the blood-red smattering of pins on an evidence board, a child’s shoe lost in the grass. But the necessity of paring down such a massive event has the effect of flattening the very elements that ought to give it its texture and heft — namely, the people involved. McCusker and Marquise, the closest thing this shifting and sprawling ensemble has to main characters, are allowed barely any room to be individuals with their own motives or personalities. Instead, they’re made to symbolize everything valiant and determined about the Scottish investigators and everything well-meaning but misguided about their American colleagues, respectively. A few of the supporting players stand out despite the vague archetypes they’re given to play — notably Peter Mullan as a wonderfully gruff police superintendent, Merritt Wever as a relentless advocate for the victims and, less favorably, Eddie Marsan affecting a bizarre Southern accent as an FBI bomb expert. But for the most part, the further the narrative strays from the search at its center, the clunkier its reliance on synecdoche becomes. An otherwise forgettable cop (James Harkness) is described as having a good memory, so that he can later bemoan this quality, so that he can stand in for every first responder traumatized by recollections of that night. A local (Phyllis Logan) spearheading the effort to return victims’ effects to their families spouts clichés like, “We just saw something that needed to be done, so we did it,” so that we can understand the entire population of Lockerbie to be generous and resolute by extension. Meanwhile, as dogged as the characters are in pursuing questions of who and how, the show is rather less interested in reflecting on what any of it means in a bigger-picture sense. We’re told the incident led to sweeping reforms in the airline industry, but not what those changes actually were. We’re informed the global implications of this crime are huge, but given no sense of what changed internationally as a result. The very existence of this show would seem to prove the bombing left a lasting impression on the Scottish psyche, but the precise contours of that impression go unexplored. If the logic is that those who lived through those days won’t need any explanation, the flaw is that four decades on, the ratio of people who clearly remember Lockerbie to those who don’t is only shrinking. Or perhaps the show’s lack of bigger answers is simply an acknowledgment that there are none, really, to be found. No amount of historical context can soothe a devastated parent’s pain. No geopolitical analysis can justify a community’s heartbreak. No outcome can bring back the lives that were ended. In that light, the bare fact that hundreds of people were murdered that day, and that hundreds more stepped up to comfort their loved ones, to bring the perpetrators to justice, to agitate for change, is worth trying to remember in itself, however imperfectly. If The Bombing of Pan Am 103 struggles to find the specific humanity of its generic characters, the impulse behind creating them in the first place — to commemorate those departed, and those who cared about them — cannot help but feel touchingly humane. THR

articles.title: ‘September Afternoon’ Dives Into the Mundane: “In an Age of Arbitrary Extraordinariness, Plain Banality Is Stimulating as F***” (Exclusive Clip)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All July 30, 2026 12:30am 'September Afternoon' Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival German filmmaker Nicolaas Schmidt has developed a following with his unique film language. If you haven’t seen any of his short- and medium-length movies yet, now may be the time. After all, his feature-length debut, September Afternoon , will world premiere on Aug. 10 in the Filmmakers of the Present Competition of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival . It marks a return to Locarno for Schmidt, whose First Time [The Time for All but Sunset — Violet] got its world premiere at the Swiss festival in 2021, where it received a Pardi di Domani special mention. Related Stories TV Disney+ Greenlights 'House of Fates,' Spinoff of Hit Korean Fortune-Telling Series 'Battle of Fates' Lifestyle Paul Newman's Daughter Clea on the Charity He Built -- and Why She'll Never Retire From It Here is what we know about September Afternoon . “A couple refuses to accept that summer is over,” a synopsis tells us. “One last time, they head to the coast, to be together between sand dunes and sea water. But the blustery autumn wind is no substitute for the cozy rays of a summer sun. Desperate struggles against the encroaching elements become a brief interlude before the situation unravels into a disaster of a different magnitude. A contemporary cosmic catastrophe.” In his work, Schmidt lets images, sounds, music and moods do the talking, while spoken words are rarely necessary. The slow passage of time in everyday situations, repetition and silences are what interest the filmmaker. And it is what he presents to the viewer in ways that make you observe and wonder. His new cinematic experience, for example, turns romantic ideas of the summer on their head to paint a contemporary portrait of longing for connection steeped in resignation. Produced by Maxi Haslberger and Balthasar Busmann, September Afternoon features cinematography by Thomas Oswald. Schmidt, who was born in Leipzig in 1979 and lives and works in Hamburg as a filmmaker, video and conceptual artist, directed and edited the film based on his own screenplay. The cast is made up of Amin Motallebzadeh, Katharina Grossmann, Hedi Grossmann and Ada Kurzhöfer. Kino Rebelde is handling international sales. “The film uses ‘dead time’ as raw material,” Schmidt says about September Afternoon in a director’s note. “I stretch mundane moments until they collapse in their emptiness — an invitation to the viewer.” And he concludes: “In an age of arbitrary extraordinariness, plain banality is stimulating as fuck.” What can we add to that? It seems like this is the perfect time to simply mention that The Hollywood Reporter can premiere an exclusive clip from September Afternoon . Watch it right here. THR

articles.title: Locarno Director Touts “Adventurous” Lineup for “Era of Algorithms” and Highlights Theme of Community
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All July 30, 2026 1:00am Giona A. Nazzaro Rosdiana Ciaravolo/Getty Images Attending the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival allows you to embark on a cinematic adventure, if you are so inclined and if you desire to do so. After all, there are all sorts of new envelope-pushing and experimental movies to explore. Or you can see the latest from your favorite auteurs. Among others, the 2026 lineup of the Swiss festival will world premiere Nowhere to Lay My Eyes , the new film from South Korean auteur Hong Sangsoo ( Right Now, Wrong Then ), who is a former Golden Leopard winner at the fest, Canadian director Denis Côté’s Nobody’s Violence , and Sixteen Moments of My Life from Spain’s Albert Serra ( Afternoons of Solitude ). Related Stories TV Disney+ Greenlights 'House of Fates,' Spinoff of Hit Korean Fortune-Telling Series 'Battle of Fates' Lifestyle Paul Newman's Daughter Clea on the Charity He Built -- and Why She'll Never Retire From It Plus, there are screen classics, such as Martin Scorsese’s Taxi Driver and David Lynch’s Wild at Heart , plus a 4K restored version of the extended director’s cut of Kevin Costner’s Dances With Wolves . Of course, Locarno will also feature star power, with 2026 fest honors set to be bestowed upon directors James Gray and Darren Aronofsky , Belgian-born actress Virginie Efira , Rick Baker, the seven-time Oscar winner behind some of cinema’s most fantastical creatures , as well as actresses Asia Argento and Isabella Rossellini . Locarno artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro , who put together the lineup for Locarno79 with his team, spoke to The Hollywood Reporter about underlying and overarching themes that audiences may notice across the program, actors as “living history of cinema,” and allowing people to be surprised and experience a sense of wonder in the age of algorithms. When you unveiled this year’s festival lineup, you called the program “adventurous.” Can you explain a little bit why that seemed such a fitting way to describe the lineup? Adventurous is the adjective that describes the experience that I was always looking forward to when I myself was visiting festivals as a cinephile or a journalist. I really wanted to explore cinema, and therefore I would go to wildly different festivals. And that is probably the reason why I’m here at Locarno today in this position. Locarno was always the festival that allowed me to be in different places at the same time. For instance, if I were to go to Venice, I would see this kind of cinema. If I were to go to Cannes, I would see that kind of cinema, and so on. For me, in a place like Locarno, you have this opportunity that if you don’t care about just a certain kind of film, you can flesh out a program where you can follow your whims and desires and inclinations, but on the other hand, if you want to explore, you can also do that. Today, in the era of algorithms that try to foresee what you will do in a week or so, simply because you clicked on a link and you read something, and then suddenly, in your feeds, this thing keeps on appearing. I wanted to create an algorithm-free experience where you can discontinue the expectations that you might have on your own behalf and push you into a situation where you can experience something else. I know this sounds very aloof, but it goes back to the possibility of being surprised, the possibility of wonder. You see a film, and you say, “Oh my God, what did I just see?” And that does not mean that you have to like it. But for me, if you are taken out of the set of conventions that usually inform your choices, that is a reward in itself. I know this also comes from a privileged point of view. I have the privilege of working with an artistic selection committee that is incredibly talented, and with our privileged viewpoint, with our gaze, we really embrace a wide spectrum of possibilities. This year’s Locarno awards go to big names again, and the lineup also features some bold names, such as Caleb Landry Jones. How do you think about the need for stars or celebrities at Locarno? I wouldn’t describe it as the need for celebrities. The history of cinema is linked to the faces of the actors that we all love: John Wayne, Marlene Dietrich, James Stewart, Bette Davis, and Katharine Hepburn. We remember these people not because they are good-looking. They are, obviously, but we remember them because they were talented people. Someone like Katharine Hepburn could read a screenplay and say, “There are 20 pages too many.” Someone like Marcello Mastroianni, who always downplayed his being this super-talented artist, had a photographic memory and could learn everything by the first read. So, we need to make a difference between talents, stars and celebrities in the way we understand them now. Because someone like Marlene Dietrich is not just a star. She is also someone who could master how to address, for instance, the collective guilt of the German-speaking people during the war after the war, and keep the memory of it while still being the greatest star on Earth. So that’s a responsibility. And for me, actors are like the living history of cinema. People remember the great films through the stories of what happened to the character in that film. We know that High Noon is a highly political film made by a European director in Hollywood at the height of the witch hunt [of McCarthyism and the Hollywood blacklist], but we remember that film because it’s been incarnated in Gary Cooper’s body. Gary Cooper’s body was the messenger of American optimism, and now suddenly you have the very same American optimism that stands alone against a whole country, against a whole city, and he needs to fight for justice. How about some of the big names that Locarno will see this year or bold names with films in high-profile spots? The talents that we are privileged to feature on the Piazza Grande are all artists, such as Olivia Wilde [whose The Invite screens on the big outdoor square in Locarno this year]. When you read an interview with Olivia Wilde, you know that she’s a cinema person who knows what she’s talking about. Caleb Landry Jones is also famous because he played [Banshee] in the X-Men [franchise], and the got a Cannes award [for best actor in 2021 for his role in Justin Kurzel’s Nitram ], but he moves between different worlds of cinema. And then, for his new film, [the Locarno-premiering Down the Arm of God , directed by Peter Brunner], he put everything at stake to work with homeless people in Texas to tell us about the plight of these people who never sleep in the same place two nights in a row and what it means to be left behind. He spent some of his time as an artist living in the shoes of someone who might not even have shoes. Also, Claes Bang, [starring in the world-premiering I Is Another , directed by Felix Randau]. How debonair can a man be? I mean, it doesn’t get more debonair than him. But every film he picks is carefully picked. He could simply be playing the good-looking man and get away with it, and nobody would complain. But the choices he makes are always against his own persona, as if he’s always questioning things: “I invite you to look beyond the surface.” The film I Is Another is basically about this – a good-looking man who claims to have done something, but did he really do it? Claes Bang always digs deeper. So it’s very bold for him to take a role like that. Overall, the fact that we tend to think of these actors and people as just good-looking faces is a bit of an unfair assessment of what they do. Ultimately, we have so many nice faces, but only the talented ones stay. Since you just mentioned a specific film – not that I want to force you to choose between movies that you all clearly felt deserve a showcase – are there any films that you were particularly excited to get or that you didn’t even think would be in this year’s Locarno lineup? There are actually quite a few films. Among others, I’m very proud to have the Italian film Ketticè , produced by Luca Guadagnino, the second film by Giovanni Tortorici, who had his first film in Venice in Orizzonti (Horizons). Then I’m particularly glad to have A Margem Do Rio ( The Riverbank ) by Enock Carvalho and Matheus Farias, close collaborators of Kleber Mendonça Filho . I’m also very happy to have Violence du Corps de l’Autre ( Nobody’s Violence) by Denis Côté. He’s coming back to fiction film, quote unquote. I’m super happy to present to the international audience Wandering Trees ( Alberi Errante ) by Salvatore Mereu, a crucial Italian filmmaker who has the breadth of a 19th-century novelist. I would also point to the film Manhunt by Wayne Wapeemukwa. That’s a true-crime film,” but it comes from a specific place in Canadian culture. The director is a descendant of the First Nations, and the film questions the colonial myth of what is beyond the frontier and how this myth still affects people. There are also other films that I’m very proud of, such as Tear Gas by Uta Beria that documents the plight of the Georgian people of standing up against the Russian infiltration of their country, or Revolutionaries Never Die , a film about the legacy of the magnificent Lebanese filmmaker Jocelyne Saab. She is this extremely interesting filmmaker. I wouldn’t call her a documentarian because she was a filmmaker, and she chronicled the Lebanese civil war. She was on the ship Atlantis when [Yasser] Arafat had to leave Lebanon and landed in Tunis, Tunisia. She also documented with an uncanny eye for the future the onset of the Iranian revolution. She was this living memory of what was going on, and the film is basically about the work and the life of Jocelyne Saab as a living archive. And [Jean-Luc] Godard himself used some of her images. When you unveiled the program for Locarno 2026 , you spoke about how several films explore the theme of community… Yes, I think that stems from a sense of being threatened and being more vulnerable. I hope this doesn’t sound sanctimonious or corny, but we live in a moment where the future could be described as the Third World War in pieces. You have the war in Ukraine and in the region formerly called the Middle East – but middle of and from where is my question. Then you have Sudan, and then you have the economic takeovers of entire regions on the African continent. Plus, there is the erasure of civil rights, political rights, individual rights. So everything is coming together at the same time. What stays is this lingering and very uncomfortable fear that you are being threatened in the individuality of what your person is, if you are not a white Western person, and you can feel how things are shifting around you. People are being singled out for what they represent to each other, and what we represent to each other is not something that we decided. It’s something that has been put on us from above by a global block of linguistic conventions of what we are. This singling out of individuals is breaking up communities, and so people are really thinking about: How can we protect our communities? How can we come together again? But “together” not in a sense of let’s just be nice and cozy, cozy. Instead, let’s think differences, let’s think individualities, let’s think heritages, let’s think bodies, let’s think sexual orientation. And how can we bring all these things together? It’s not easy, but it’s exactly the thing that all these wars are threatening to suffocate. All these conversations that we need to have are being threatened. In a community, there is the opportunity, the possibility to speak, to talk, to make films, and to make a film is to engage with someone else to say: “What do you think about this?” Can we have a back-and-forth? So, communities today are the last vanguard of what it is to have and care about human dignity. Communities today are the laboratories where we can still think about how to make it all together. THR

articles.title: Matthew Macfadyen, Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls Romance ‘You Are Here’
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All July 30, 2026 1:32am The British actors will play Michael and Marnie, respectively. Josh Wool/Juankr Logo text Matthew Macfadyen and Claire Foy will star in You Are Here , an eight-part adaptation of David Nicholls’ acclaimed, best-selling novel of the same name. The BBC and Starz have greenlit the series, directed by Lenny Abrahamson ( Normal People ) and produced by Element Pictures. Succession alum Macfadyen and The Crown ‘s Foy will lead the cast as Michael and Marnie, respectively. When a mutual friend throws them together, the pair unexpectedly find themselves setting off on an epic walk. Related Stories Movies Locarno Director Touts "Adventurous" Lineup for "Era of Algorithms" and Highlights Theme of Community Movies 'September Afternoon' Dives Into the Mundane: "In an Age of Arbitrary Extraordinariness, Plain Banality Is Stimulating as F***" (Exclusive Clip) Against the odds, they end up on the brink of a relationship that neither was looking for, but which might be exactly the one they both need. Michael and Marnie go coast-to-coast across the stunning — and soaking — English countryside, navigating an undeniable attraction that is as exhilarating as it is terrifying. “I’m so delighted to be working on You Are Here with Element, the BBC, Starz and Lenny, whose work I’ve admired for many years,” said Nicholls, who also wrote the widely adapted One Day . “Matthew and Claire are both just dream casting, wonderful in comedy and drama, so detailed and thoughtful and sympathetic. The intention with the novel was to write a close-up study of a relationship, but set against this magnificent landscape, and that’s our ambition here too; to make something both intimate and epic, funny and dramatic, a romantic comedy with real emotion.” Abrahamson added that the story is ultimately “deeply hopeful.” He said: “As a huge admirer of David’s writing, I’m delighted to be collaborating with him to bring You Are Here to the screen. The novel is such a beautiful love story — funny, profound and ultimately deeply hopeful. I’m also extremely excited to have Claire and Matthew, two actors I hugely admire, playing Michael and Marnie.” Both Nicholls and Abrahamson also serve as executive producers alongside Foy and MacFadyen, Ed Guiney, Andrew Lowe and Emma Norton for Element Pictures and Jonny Richards and Anna Ferguson for the BBC. The series is produced by Clare Shepherd. Global sales will be handled by Fremantle with De Maio Entertainment spearheading the partnership with Starz. Set along the Coast to Coast walking trail from the Lake District to Robin Hood’s Bay in North Yorkshire, U.K., You Are Here will be filmed in the Lake District and around Manchester. THR

articles.title: Opposition Grows to FIFA World Cup Sell-Off Plan
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All July 30, 2026 2:29am FIFA President Gianni Infantino Catherine Ivill - AMA/Getty Images Pushback to a controversial plan put forward by FIFA boss Gianni Infantino to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other commercial operations to private investors is growing. European soccer governing body UEFA has called an emergency meeting of its members on Thursday to discuss a coordinated response to the plan, with a European boycott of FIFA tournaments among the options being discussed. UEFA has condemned Infantino’s proposal, calling it a plan to “sell the soul” of football. Other major regional soccer bodies, including the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which covers North and Central America as well as the Caribbean confederations, have also criticized the proposals, saying they were not consulted on the plan and only became aware of it through the media. Related Stories TV Matthew Macfadyen, Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls Romance 'You Are Here' Movies Locarno Director Touts "Adventurous" Lineup for "Era of Algorithms" and Highlights Theme of Community The plan would see FIFA set up a new entity, called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), that would bundle all the money-making operations associated with the soccer World Cup — including broadcast rights, sponsorship, ticket sales and licensing fees — and sell a significant stake in the new operation to private investors. Thrive Capital, an investment company founded by Joshua Kushner, brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is leading the search for investors. FIFA is valuing the FFE at around $20 billion and has said the plan to sell equity stakes in the commercial group could raise an additional $10 billion for its member organizations. Those members, the 211 national soccer associations that make up FIFA, would have to vote to approve the proposal. The opposition by UEFA, Concacaf, and the AFC suggests Infantino could have a fight on his hands. Together, those three confederations make up 143 of the 211 FIFA members. But opposition to the FFE is not a unified front. In Europe, Czechia’s soccer association has backed the plan. Despite the AFC’s disapproval, association member Saudi Arabia is also believed to support it. Saudi Arabia will host the 2024 World Cup and the Saudi soccer association is a close ally of Infantino. It is not clear whether the FIFA plan can pass with a simple majority vote or if the proposal requires a change to FIFA statutes, which necessitates a 75 percent majority. Infantino released a video on Wednesday evening calling the FFE “a proposal, an offer,” that would be subject to a democratic and consultation process. “It is an opportunity but not an ­obligation,” he said. “It is a golden opportunity to turbocharge the development of the game globally.” That “golden opportunity” will come with payments to FIFA members. FIFA has given members until Sept. 19 to decide whether to apply for an initial payment of $20 million from the proposed sell-off. In a statement, UEFA said the $20 million payoff “says everything you need to know about this plan” and accused FIFA of “using our sport to enrich themselves and their friends.” Concacaf and the AFC have not been as sharp in their criticism, but in a statement Concacaf said they were “deeply concerned by the lack of due process,” noting Concacaf “was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release.” The AFC issued a similar statement, saying they were “not consulted on the proposal and [are] disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it through the appropriate and established governance channels. While the AFC recognizes the importance of exploring innovative approaches that can strengthen the future of global football, initiatives of this scale and consequence must be founded upon the principles of good governance, transparency and meaningful consultation.” FIFA is could also face a backlash from elite clubs. The European Football Clubs organization, which represents more than 850 clubs, complained they were also not consulted on the FFE plan. “The EFC learned about this proposal in the same way as most global football stakeholders – without warning and through the media.” UEFA could vote to boycott upcoming FIFA tournaments, including next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil, though that is considered an extreme option and could be seen as unduly punishing the women’s game for a proposal which is primarily focused on monetizing the men’s World Cup and men’s Club World Cup. THR

articles.title: Zoe Saldaña to Receive Locarno Fest Special Honor
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All July 30, 2026 3:12am Zoe Saldaña Frazer Harrison/WireImage Zoe Saldaña ( Guardians of the Galaxy , Emilia Pérez , Lioness ) will be among the stars attending the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival . On Monday, Aug. 10, she will feature in a special conversation with the public where she will also be awarded a Special Pardo, or Special Leopard honor, organizers said on Thursday. Italian musician Claudio Simonetti ( Suspiria, Dawn of the Dead ), the keyboardist of the progressive rock band Goblin who has specialized in creating the scores for Italian and U.S. horror films since the 1970s, will also be honored “for his legendary contribution to music in film.” He will receive his honor on Thursday, Aug. 6 ahead of a special screening of Cut and Run ( Inferno in diretta ). Related Stories Business Opposition Grows to FIFA World Cup Sell-Off Plan TV Matthew Macfadyen, Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls Romance 'You Are Here' Movie premieres across the big Swiss summer film festival are also set to draw a wide array of big-name talent to Locarno. The fest on Thursday highlighted the expected presence of the likes of Olivia Wilde ( The Invite ), Monica Bellucci ( Ketticè ), Isabelle Huppert ( Ni vue, ni connue ), Claes Bang and Valerie Pachner ( I Is Another ), Caleb Landry Jones ( Down the Arm of God ), Kingsley Ben-Adir and Rob Morgan ( Frank & Louis ), Anders Danielsen Lie, Kathrine Thorborg Johansen and Simon Sears ( Brave New Love ), Ingrid Caven ( Sixteen Moments of My Life ) and Theo Rossi ( Bruton ) . Locarno 2026 has previously set honors for U.S. directors James Gray and Darren Aronofsky , Belgian-born actress Virginie Efira , Rick Baker, the seven-time Oscar winner behind some of cinema’s most fantastical creatures , Sigurjón “Joni” Sighvatsson, the producer behind the likes of Twin Peaks , Wild at Heart and Beverly Hills, 90210 , as well as actresses Asia Argento and Isabella Rossellini . Other names set to attend Locarno include Sandrine Kiberlain ( Ni vue, ni connue ), Valerio Mastandrea ( Armony ), Emmanuelle Devos ( Demain je tombe amoureux ), Kim Minhee (Nowhere to Lay My Eyes) , Giulia Maenza ( Alberi erranti ), Alessandro Haber ( Cercatori d’angeli ), and Sara Serraiocco ( Il Cileno ). The 79th edition of the Locarno festival runs Aug. 5-15. THR

articles.title: Netflix and AMC Global Media Ink $500 Million ‘Walking Dead’ Streaming Deal
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All July 30, 2026 4:06am 'The Walking Dead' Jackson Lee Davis/AMC AMC Global Media and Netflix have inked a major five-year, $500 million global streaming rights deal for The Walking Dead Universe. The deal will bring all six spin-off series to Netflix starting next year, creating a unified destination for the franchise, and it will be non-exclusive, meaning that AMC+ will get the original series for the first time in 2027. AMC announced the deal in connection with its quarterly earnings report Thursday morning. While the original Walking Dead has been on Netflix since 2011, the new five-year deal will also expand the show to new territories, including the U.K., Italy, Australia, New Zealand. Related Stories Movies Zoe Saldaña to Receive Locarno Fest Special Honor Business Opposition Grows to FIFA World Cup Sell-Off Plan The new deal covers some 371 episodes of TV between The Walking Dead , Fear the Walking Dead , The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon , The Walking Dead: Dead City , The Walking Dead: The Ones Who Live , The Walking Dead: World Beyond and Tales of The Walking Dead , with the shows debuting in different territories as their streaming licenses kick in over the course of next year. “Audiences have discovered and loved The Walking Dead on Netflix for nearly 15 years and the show continues to attract new fans,” said Lori Conkling, vp of licensing at Netflix. “We’re excited to partner with AMC Global Media to continue to expand that access to more audiences around the world and bring the entirety of The Walking Dead Universe to Netflix.” “We are thrilled to expand our long-time partnership with Netflix around The Walking Dead , ” said Kristin Dolan, CEO of AMC Global Media. “This deal creates a global destination for this universe – all shows, all episodes – making the franchise more accessible than ever to fans around the world. In addition, the co-exclusive agreement allows us to bring the original series to AMC+ for the first time early next year. Netflix has been an important partner in making The Walking Dead one of the most successful franchises in the history of entertainment. This agreement is a fantastic result for our companies, for the fans and for this timeless IP.” THR

articles.title: Joyce Carol Oates Defends ‘The Odyssey’ and Slams Translator for Scathing Review: ‘Speaks in the Crude Language of MAGA Folks’
articles.full_text: Jul 29, 2026 8:00pm PT Joyce Carol Oates Defends ‘The Odyssey’ and Slams Translator for Scathing Review: ‘Speaks in the Crude Language of MAGA Folks’ By Jack Dunn Plus Icon Jack Dunn Latest Ian McKellen Discovered Anthony Mackie Is the New Captain America on ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Set and Told Him: ‘You Deserve That’ 12 hours ago Zendaya Stuns ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Premiere in ‘Abstract’ Spider-Inspired Look: ‘It’s Like This Metamorphosis’ 2 days ago ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’s’ Breakout, Ryan Reynolds’ Jeanpool Stunt and More Comic-Con Highlights 2 days ago See All Universal Pictures Author Joyce Carol Oates came to the defense of Christopher Nolan ’s “ The Odyssey ” after translator Emily Wilson wrote a viral review attacking the film. “Rather than disagreeing with interpretations of Homer in a collegial manner, this person, who has benefited enormously from Nolan’s film, speaks in the crude language of MAGA folks attacking someone with ideas that differ from hers,” Carol wrote on X. “One would expect a translator, of all people, beholden to a text, in service to a text, to be just a wee bit more thoughtful & respectful of others who are acting in good faith just as (she would claim) she is.” Related Stories 'A Star Is Born' Producer Lynette Howell Taylor Re-Elected Academy President Hollywood Can't Survive Without Animation. So Why Won't the Industry Respect It? Wilson, who translated a 2017 version of Homer’s “The Odyssey,” slammed Nolan’s take in a review for the London Review of Books. She wrote that the film lacked “psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth” and had “nothing convincing to say.” Popular on Variety Wilson’s review reads, “I had hoped that Nolan’s affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters. But ‘The Odyssey’ features his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality … the film’s vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants.” She later added, “The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has a convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible.” Nolan previously praised Wilson for her translation of the ancient text. articles.title: Thanh Hang, Hong Anh’s Vietnamese Period Drama ‘Madame in Saigon’ Lands North American Rights Deal With Reel Citrus, Live On (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Jul 29, 2026 11:55pm PT Thanh Hang, Hong Anh’s Vietnamese Period Drama ‘Madame in Saigon’ Lands North American Rights Deal With Reel Citrus, Live On (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Ramayana’ Trailer: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash Face Off in First Part of Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Project Market Unveils 30 Selections for 2026 Edition 4 hours ago Thanh Hang, Hong Anh’s Vietnamese Period Drama ‘Madame in Saigon’ Lands North American Rights Deal With Reel Citrus, Live On (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All Reel Citrus/Live On Reel Citrus has acquired North American rights to the Vietnamese period drama “Mesdames Thanh Sắc,” which it will release as “ Madame in Saigon ,” through a partnership with Ho Chi Minh City-based production and rights partner Live On. Directed by Thắng Vũ, “Madame in Saigon” is set in 1960s Saigon and follows dancer Cầm Thanh (Thanh Hằng) as she rises through the city’s nightlife into a power struggle with Madame Sắc (Hồng Ánh), owner of the Kim Đô nightclub. The cast also includes Lương Thế Thành and singer-actor Văn Mai Hương. The film opened in Vietnam in June. Related Stories Christopher Nolan's Oscar 'Odyssey': Can Matt Damon, Monsters and Mythology Deliver Another Best Picture Statue? BAFTA Tweaks Film Awards Rules, Expands Outstanding British Film Longlist and Updates AI Guidance Reel Citrus will hold a red-carpet premiere in Los Angeles on Aug. 26, with Thanh Hằng in attendance. The actor rose to fame as Vietnam’s preeminent supermodel in the 2010s before moving into dramatic film roles, with credits including “Mẹ chồng” (“Mother-in-Law”) and “Những cô gái chân dài.” She has also served as a longtime judge on “Vietnam’s Next Top Model.” Popular on Variety Following the premiere, Thanh Hằng will join a press junket in Orange County alongside local community organizations. The wider campaign will extend across digital platforms and include creator support, as well as Vietnamese Student Associations across the U.S. and Canada. “‘Madame in Saigon’ is exactly the kind of story we built Reel Citrus to champion, bold, unapologetically Vietnamese, and made to travel,” said Brittany Tran, executive director of Reel Citrus. “Our job is to build the audience around the film to make sure our communities see themselves on screen and show up for each other. Partnering with Live On to bring this film and Thanh Hằng to North American audiences is a milestone for us, and just the beginning,” Tran added. Founded in 2025, Reel Citrus has previously led theatrical marketing campaigns for “Leaving Mom” and “Ancestral Home.” Its next release, “Summer School, 2001,” is slated for October. The deal marks Live On’s first U.S. collaboration and its debut in the North American theatrical market. The Ho Chi Minh City studio has spent more than a decade producing multi-genre Vietnamese films. The film opens across North America on Aug. 28. articles.title: Busan’s Asian Project Market Unveils 30 Selections for 2026 Edition
articles.full_text: Jul 30, 2026 12:29am PT Busan’s Asian Project Market Unveils 30 Selections for 2026 Edition By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Ramayana’ Trailer: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash Face Off in First Part of Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Project Market Unveils 30 Selections for 2026 Edition 4 hours ago Thanh Hang, Hong Anh’s Vietnamese Period Drama ‘Madame in Saigon’ Lands North American Rights Deal With Reel Citrus, Live On (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All Cheyne Gateley/Variety Busan’s Asian Project Market (APM) has unveiled the 30 feature projects selected for its 2026 edition. APM set a new all-time submissions record for the third consecutive year, receiving 604 entries from 48 countries. That marked an increase of 149 submissions year-on-year, following 455 submissions from 44 countries in 2025, 441 from 44 countries in 2024 and 399 from 50 countries in 2023. Submissions from Asia reached 423, up 82 from the previous year, while Korean submissions rose to 137, up 58. Related Stories Anne Hathaway's Oscars 'Odyssey': Will She Campaign for Lead Actress or Supporting? Oscar Voters Rave Over Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' at First Academy Screenings: ‘The Definitive Filmmaker of Our Time’ From that pool, 30 projects representing 20 countries were selected. The lineup spans courtroom drama, coming-of-age story, family drama, crime thriller, queer romantic comedy, black comedy and mystery thriller, with the selected works touching on social realities, personal identity, family relationships and ethical tensions within communities. The slate mixes feature debuts from emerging filmmakers with new projects from directors already recognized on the festival circuit. Popular on Variety Three Japanese projects made the cut: “13” from Mori Tatsuya, who claimed BIFF’s New Currents prize in 2023 for “September 1923”; “Wings of Return (working title)” from Hirose Nanako; and “Yours” from Igarashi Kohei. Central and South Asian filmmakers also feature prominently. Kyrgyzstan’s Dastan Zhapar Ryskeldi joins APM for a third time with “Bosogo,” while Sri Lanka’s Prasanna Vithanage presents “Islands,” following “Paradise,” which took the Jiseok prize at BIFF in 2023. India’s Dominic Sangma brings “Veil of Dust,” examining tragic contradictions within a community, and Tribeny Rai returns with her second project, “A Chronicle of Minor Things” (working title). Rounding out the region are Payal Sethi’s “Babak,” Stenzin Tankyong’s feature debut “Idiot (Kakthet)” and Pakistani director Eshah Shakeel’s feature debut “Dancers.” China, Hong Kong and Taiwan contributed four selections, pairing emerging filmmakers with experienced producers. Tibetan director Kangdrun presents “Orlo in the House,” Wang Zhiyi brings feature debut “Unripe,” Hong Kong’s So Chak Long enters with “Whisper of the Silence” and Taiwan’s Yen Hao-hsuan makes his first feature with “Uncle.” Southeast and West Asian entries include Aditya Ahmad’s feature directorial debut “Goldfish.” Ahmad previously took the top short-film prize in Venice’s Horizons sidebar in 2018. Reza Rahadian Matulessy follows debut feature “On Your Lap,” which picked up three prizes in BIFF’s Vision – Asia sidebar in 2025, with second feature “Casparina.” Cambodia’s Chheangkea has his first feature, “Little Phnom Penh,” selected, while the Philippines’ E Del Mundo brings “Once Upon a Time in the Philippines” and Iran’s Mehrnoush Alia presents “Bon Voyage.” Singapore’s Alvin Lee offers black comedy “Talk To Me When You Are Dead,” and Malaysia’s Tan Seng Kiat presents “One Fine Day,” which took the APM Next prize at TCCF 2025. Also selected are Thailand’s Panu Aree with “Fātimah” and Indonesia’s Mouly Surya with “The Wife Who Can See Dead People (Or Jinn).” Seven Korean projects round out the slate. Lee Sangcheol, whose films “Jesus Hospital,” “The Snob” and “Blesser” have all screened at BIFF, presents “PARK Deul-bi.” Choi Hyunyoung, whose “Memories of a Dead End” played in Korean Cinema Today – Panorama, brings “All’s Well That Ends Well,” and Lee Hanju, whose debut feature “The Waves of Winter” screened in the Korean Cinema Today – Vision strand, presents “The Family Table.” The remaining Korean selections are Park Syeyoung’s “Satellite of Love,” Park Joonho’s “Kuroshio” (Park also directed “3670”), actor-director Ryu Hyunkyung’s “Dog Fight” and novelist-filmmaker Kim Jinyeong’s “Red Hunger”; Kim previously directed “The Other Child.” The seven projects span psychological thriller, queer romantic comedy, black comedy, mystery thriller and drama. Selected projects will be nominated for awards backed by sponsors. ACFM is the official market of the Busan International Film Festival and is held in Busan every October. The 2025 edition, ACFM’s 20th, drew industry professionals from 55 countries – 3,024 of them, alongside 1,222 registered companies – with on-site attendance reaching a record 30,006. The Sales Market tallied 8,438 business meetings, generating an estimated $71.1 million in transactions. The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs Oct. 6-15, with the 21st ACFM held Oct. 10-13. articles.title: Mubi to Release ‘La Mesías,’ From ‘La Bola Negra’ Cannes Best Director Winners, in the U.K., Germany, Canada, Australia and Beyond (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Jul 30, 2026 1:21am PT Mubi to Release ‘La Mesías,’ From ‘La Bola Negra’ Cannes Best Director Winners, in the U.K., Germany, Canada, Australia and Beyond (EXCLUSIVE) Created by Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, ‘La Mesías’ is hailed by its fans as one of the greatest shows made in Spain in its recent golden age of film and TV By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest San Sebastián New Directors: Billy Lumby, Marlene Emilie Lyngstad, ‘Money Heist’ Star Jaime Lorente and More 27 minutes ago EFD Studios Names José Miguel Álvarez Ibargüengoitia CEO, EFD Studios Mexico (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago San Sebastián Lineup: Pablo Larraín, Mike Leigh, Benjamín Naishtat and More 2 days ago See All La Mesías Courtesy Mubi “La Mesías,” the multi-prized series created by Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo , behind the Cannes best-director winning “ La bola negra ,” will be released by Mubi in U.K., Canada, Turkey, the Netherlands, Germany and Austria and Australia, streaming exclusively from Sept. 3. A Movistar Plus Original, produced in collaboration with Ambrossi and Calvo’s label Suma Content, “La Mesías” will also stream on Mubi in France, Mubi announced Thursday. The deal was closed with Movistar Plus International. Mubi will launch with a two-episode premiere. Related Stories Christopher Nolan's Oscar 'Odyssey': Can Matt Damon, Monsters and Mythology Deliver Another Best Picture Statue? Hollywood Can't Survive Without Animation. So Why Won't the Industry Respect It? A step-up from “Veneno,” which made a splash on HBO in the U.S., six-part series “La Mesías” delivered a example of the full-on ambition of Los Javis, as Ambrossi and Calvo are known in Spain, which was seen again in “La bola negra,” one of the highest-profile Cannes main competition contenders which sparked rave reviews, and a bidding war for the U.S. rights. Popular on Variety “La Mesías,” Los Javis’ title just prior to “La bola negra,” begins with thirtysomething loner Enric watching a viral video of Stella Maris, a Christian pop band. His reaction? He literally wets himself. For the singers are his younger sisters. Memories flood back of his own childhood and youth, traumatized by his parents’ religious fanaticism which climaxes in mother Montse declaring herself the daughter of God, and that the words her daughters sing are dictated to her by God and part of her mission to save humanity via music. Enric escaped. He now determines to save his sisters. Action flashes back and forward from a present-day 2013 to the 1980s when Enric and slightly younger sister Irene are kids, to around 1997, catching them in their late teens. The production shot for 25 weeks totally on location, mostly at 30 rural sites outside Barcelona. The series featured 170 characters and 3,800 extras. 1980s flashbacks are sometimes lensed in 16 mm, capturing the impressionism of memory. The series genre hops: Episode 1 blends psychodrama and sci-fi, for example. Ep. 2 has a procedural pulse; Episode 3 works like a real-life musical. For all its style, the series delivers a powerful sense of the importance of family education. To mark Mubi’s release announcement, it has shared with Variety a new international trailer, which captures Enric (Roger Casamayor, “Pan’s Labyrinth”) as he seeks out sister Irene (Macarena García), literally scarred by the past, to help him rescue his sisters, plus the presentation of an early video, “lyrics by God,” says one little sister, and later bizarre Christian pop rap, created by Spanish underground duo Carlos Ballesteros and Genís Segarra. Rosalía producer Raül Refree composed the series’ original soundtrack. Messianic matriarch Montse is played at different ages by Ana Rujas (“Cardo”), Cannes best actress winner Lola Dueñas (“Volver,” “La bola negra”) and Carmen Machi, star of Series Mania winner “Celeste.” “It’s very difficult to unlearn what you’ve been taught – I’m talking about education – the past resounds in your body for ever. That touches me in many ways. As a son, a member of the LGBT collective. The series talks about religion, but as a form of education and this is what makes it interesting,” Javier Calvo said on a Variety set visit to the isolated family house, hidden in wooded mountains south of Barcelona. “La Mesías” world premiered at San Sebastián Festival in 2023, where it gleaned glowing reviews. It went on to become the first Spanish series to be selected for the Sundance Festival, win direction and a Student Audience Award at Series Mania and, released by Arte France, be hailed by La Liberation as “one of the most beautiful series of the year.” Picked up off Cannes by Netflix, “La bola negra” is now being positioned as an awards contender. articles.full_text: Jul 30, 2026 1:27am PT ‘Balcanica,’ Starring Matilda De Angelis, Picked Up by M-Appeal Ahead of Venice World Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) The film follows two Afghan musicians, father and son, as they travel across the Balkans By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest ‘Balcanica,’ Starring Matilda De Angelis, Picked Up by M-Appeal Ahead of Venice World Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago World Cup Boycott Proposed as Opposition to Controversial FIFA Private Investment Plan Grows 24 hours ago Diego Luna to Be Feted at Sarajevo Film Festival as ‘Ashes’ Screens 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Nightswim Berlin-based sales outfit M-Appeal has picked up international sales rights to Nicola Sorcinelli ‘s “Balcanica,” starring Matilda De Angelis , which will have its world premiere in competition at the 23rd Giornate degli Autori, also known as Venice Days, held alongside the 83rd Venice Intl. Film Festival. “Balcanica” follows the journey of the orchestra conductor Nasar and his tuba-playing son Jalil across the Balkans, after leaving Afghanistan, where music has been banned. Their path eventually crosses that of Greta, an Italian doctor whose empathy and resilience shine through the situation. As their journeys continue to intertwine, the three must face the life changing choices the moment demands. Related Stories Anne Hathaway's Oscars 'Odyssey': Will She Campaign for Lead Actress or Supporting? Christopher Nolan's Oscar 'Odyssey': Can Matt Damon, Monsters and Mythology Deliver Another Best Picture Statue? The film stars Italian actress Matilda De Angelis, known for her leading role in the Netflix series “The Law According to Lidia Poët,” Silver Bear winner Babak Karimi, celebrated for his performance in Asghar Farhadi’s “A Separation,” winner of the Golden Bear at the 2011 Berlinale and the 2012 Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, and rising talent Ivar Wafaei. The screenplay is written by Sorcinelli and Andrea Brusa. Popular on Variety “Balcanica” is produced by Nightswim and Fremantle’s Wildside, in co-production with This and That Productions and Antitalent, and in association with M74 and Nieminen Film. Sorcinelli said that “Balcanica,” her debut feature film, is “a story about a vital journey, denied freedoms and the deeply human need to keep searching for one’s place in the world. articles.title: Matthew Macfadyen and Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls’ ‘You Are Here’ for BBC and Starz
articles.full_text: Jul 30, 2026 1:34am PT Matthew Macfadyen and Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls’ ‘You Are Here’ for BBC and Starz By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Matthew Macfadyen and Claire Foy to Lead Adaptation of David Nicholls’ ‘You Are Here’ for BBC and Starz 2 hours ago Ewan McGregor and Alan Cumming to Lead Scottish Stage Adaptation of Harry Macqueen’s Gay Romantic Drama ‘Supernova’ 19 hours ago Jared Leto Says ‘I Have Never Sexually Assaulted Anyone’ Amid New Allegations: ‘These Claims Are Categorically False’ 19 hours ago See All Josh Wool, Juankr Matthew Macfadyen and Claire Foy are to lead the TV adaptation of “You Are Here,” the bestselling novel by “One Day” author David Nicholls. The 8-part series — which was first announced by Variety earlier this year — has been green lit by the BBC and Starz, with Lenny Abrahamson directing, reuniting with the BBC for the first time since “Normal People.” Set to be filmed around in the Lake District and around Manchester, “You Are Here,” is being produced by the Fremantle-owned Irish powerhouse Element Pictures, who also produced “Normal People.” Global sales will be handled by Fremantle with De Maio Entertainment spearheading the partnership with Starz. Related Stories EA's 'Skate.' to Launch X Games-Themed In-Game Event (Gaming News Roundup) Set along the Coast to Coast walking trail from the Lake District to Robin Hood’s Bay in North Yorkshire, “You Are Here” follows Michael (Macfadyen) and Marnie (Foy), strangers thrown together by a mutual friend who unexpectedly find themselves setting off on an epic walk. Against the odds, they end up on the brink of a relationship that neither was looking for, but which might be exactly the one they both need. Popular on Variety The series is “about finding a connection when you least expect it and overcoming the obstacles of midlife,” reads the description. “Treading the tricky path from loneliness to love, Marnie and Michael go coast-to-coast across the stunning (and sometimes soaking) English countryside, navigating an undeniable attraction that is as exhilarating as it is terrifying.” “I’m so delighted to be working on ‘You Are Here’ with Element, the BBC, Starz and Lenny, whose work I’ve admired for many years,” said Nicholls, who adapted his own novel. “And Matthew and Claire are both just dream casting, wonderful in comedy and drama, so detailed and thoughtful and sympathetic. The intention with the novel was to write a close-up study of a relationship, but set against this magnificent landscape, and that’s our ambition here too; to make something both intimate and epic, funny and dramatic, a romantic comedy with real emotion. We can’t wait to bring Marnie and Michael’s journey to the screen.” Added Abrahamson: “As a huge admirer of David’s writing, I’m delighted to be collaborating with him to bring ‘You Are Here’ to the screen. The novel is such a beautiful love story – funny, profound and ultimately deeply hopeful. I’m also extremely excited to have Claire and Matthew, two actors I hugely admire, playing Michael and Marnie.” “You Are Here” is an Element Pictures, a Fremantle company, production for the BBC and Starz. Both Abrahamson and Nicholls serve as executive producers alongside Claire Foy and MacFadyen, Ed Guiney, Andrew Lowe and Emma Norton for Element Pictures and Jonny Richards and Anna Ferguson for the BBC. The series is produced by Clare Shepherd. articles.title: Giorgio Armani Series in the Works From Fremantle-Owned Lux Vide and Iconic Designer’s Fashion House (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: Jul 30, 2026 2:00am PT Giorgio Armani Series in the Works From Fremantle-Owned Lux Vide and Iconic Designer’s Fashion House (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Giorgio Armani Series in the Works From Fremantle-Owned Lux Vide and Iconic Designer’s Fashion House (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Reply AI Film Festival Unveils Jury Featuring ‘The Lion King’ Director Rob Minkoff, ‘Twilight’ Helmer Catherine Hardwicke and More 2 days ago Venice Chief Alberto Barbera Under Fire for Lack of Female Directors in Competition: ‘It Is a One-Dimensional Selection’ 3 days ago See All Courtesy Armani/Fremantle The life and career of Giorgio Armani is set to be the subject of a high-end TV series produced by Italy’s Lux Vide, which is collaborating with the fashion house founded by the iconic designer known for his close ties to Hollywood. The still-untitled Armani biopic series — which will be tailored for the international market — has enlisted Turkish-born Italy-based director Ferzan Ozpetek , who is known for combining artistic depth with box-office appeal. Related Stories EA's 'Skate.' to Launch X Games-Themed In-Game Event (Gaming News Roundup) Ozpetek, who knew Armani personally, recently scored a global hit with the 2025 crowdpleaser “Diamonds,” about a group of warm-hearted women in a Rome atelier rushing to fulfill a demanding order from an Oscar-winning costume designer client in the 1970s. “Diamonds” scored mightily at the box local office and traveled widely. Ozpetek’s TV experience includes 2022’s first Disney+ Italian original series “The Ignorant Angels,” a romantic drama spun off from his local hit “Ignorant Fairies.” Popular on Variety “I knew, admired and spent time with Giorgio for many years, both on official occasions and in more private settings,” Ozpetek said in a statement to Variety. “We talked about cinema, of which he was notably passionate and an expert. But also about art, costumes, architecture, and, I would say, life itself. I could see within him a visionary and a brilliant artist. But also a down-to-earth and very determined man.” The director added: “The opportunity to tell his story is both an exciting honor and a challenge that involves capturing the many facets of such a complex, original and captivating personality.” Ozpetek is co-writing the screenplay for the Armani series in collaboration with Lux Vide’s head writer Francesco Arlanch, whose credits include Lux’s widely exported series “Medici,” “Hotel Costiera” and medical drama “Doc.” Storylines and series structure are being kept under wraps. Known globally as the Milan-based fashion pioneer with piercing blue eyes and a vision that combined laid back elegance and attention to detail, Armani first made his mark with the unlined men’s sports jackets and deconstructed suits worn by Richard Gere in 1980 in “American Gigolo.” But Armani also reimagined the woman’s power suit. He dressed scores of Hollywood’s female stars including Julia Roberts, Diane Keaton, Jodie Foster, Cate Blanchett, Lupita Nyong’o, Anne Hathaway and Michelle Yeoh in both minimalist attire — such as the Armani men’s suit famously worn by Julia Roberts when she won a Golden Globe for “Steel Magnolias” in 1990 — and glittery gowns like the “Nairobi blue” crystal-encrusted sequin gown worn by Lupita Nyong’o at the 2024 Academy Awards. The long list of male actors who regularly wore Armani on red carpets, and also on screen, comprises Leonardo DiCaprio, George Clooney Russell Crowe, Robert De Niro and Tom Cruise, to name a few. His Hollywood connection earned Armani wardrobe film credits in more than 200 movies. Armani — a self-made man who fully owned his $10 billion fashion empire at the time of his death on Sept. 4, 2025 at age 91 – was known to often appear in dark trousers and his trademark black T-shirt. He was born in the northern Italian town of Piacenza on July 11, 1934. After two decades in the fashion industry starting in 1957, he and his partner Sergio Galeotti sold their Volkswagen for $10,000 to start up their own menswear ready-to-wear label. They launched both men’s and women’s lines the following year. Fiercely private, Armani rarely discussed his personal life. He did tell Vanity Fair that he had romances with both men and women. He was in long-term relationship with Galeotti until his AIDS-related death in 1985. The Giorgio Armani fashion house has agreed to support production of the Fremantle TV series, providing access to its “archives, creations and iconic locations, offering an unparalleled insight into the world and legacy of one of fashion’s most influential figures,” according to a Fremantle statement. “For years, Lux had been chasing the dream of telling the world the story of Giorgio Armani, an artist who invented a unique and recognizeable style,” Lux Vide founder and president Matilde Bernabei said in a statement. She went on to describe Armani as “a standard-bearer of Made in Italy who rewrote the rules of style and elegance.” “It will be an ambitious series,” Bernabei added, “and we are proud to know that the market has immediately embraced this project with interest, enthusiastically confirming its international potential.” Giorgio Armani and Ferzan Ozpetek Stefano Guindani/Courtesy Armani Trumps Received $10.7 Million Fee for Amazon’s ‘Melania’ Documentary Taylor Swift Reveals Original Song for ‘Toy Story 5’: ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’ — a ‘Return to Country’ Lesley Manville Joins Brett Goldstein in Amazon Comedy Series ‘Escorted’ Spike Lee, Adam Sandler, Ben Stiller, Larry David, Timothée Chalamet and More Watch New York Knicks Pull Off Biggest Comeback in NBA Finals History Taylor Swift Performs ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’ at ‘Toy Story 5’ Premiere, Says Movie Is a ‘Masterpiece’ ‘Carrie’ TV Series: First-Look Images From Mike Flanagan’s Take on Stephen King Classic Loading comments...
