articles.title: ‘Ramayana’ Trailer: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash Face Off in First Part of Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic
articles.full_text: Jul 30, 2026 2:53am PT ‘Ramayana’ Trailer: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash Face Off in First Part of Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Ramayana’ Trailer: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash Face Off in First Part of Nitesh Tiwari’s Epic 1 hour ago Busan’s Asian Project Market Unveils 30 Selections for 2026 Edition 4 hours ago Thanh Hang, Hong Anh’s Vietnamese Period Drama ‘Madame in Saigon’ Lands North American Rights Deal With Reel Citrus, Live On (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All Prime Focus Studios The first trailer for “ Ramayana ” has debuted, marking the most substantial promotional asset yet for Nitesh Tiwari ‘s two-part adaptation of the ancient Hindu epic, ahead of a worldwide release this November. The story follows exiled prince Rama ( Ranbir Kapoor ) and his consort Sita (Sai Pallavi) through exile into catastrophe, as Sita’s abduction at the hands of Ravana ( Yash ) sets in motion an epic war between righteousness and evil. Part 1 is expected to culminate with the abduction itself, leaving the rescue campaign and the climactic battle for Part 2. Both parts are filmed for Imax. The two films together are budgeted at approximately $500 million, Variety understands. Related Stories Anne Hathaway's Oscars 'Odyssey': Will She Campaign for Lead Actress or Supporting? Oscar Voters Rave Over Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' at First Academy Screenings: ‘The Definitive Filmmaker of Our Time’ The long-awaited trailer offers a sweeping first look at the Hindi-language spectacle, which will also be dubbed into several other languages. Popular on Variety The preview opens with an introduction to demon king Ravana asserting his dominion across the three realms of heaven, earth, and the underworld. A voiceover establishes the overarching mythological conflict, explaining how Lord Vishnu takes human form to restore righteousness on earth when chaos threatens the universe, introducing Kapoor’s Prince Rama as King Dasharatha’s (Arun Govil) eldest son. The trailer shifts focus to Rama’s 14-year exile to the forest to uphold his father’s vow, accompanied by his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana (played by Ravi Dubey). The peaceful exile is shattered when Ravana’s sister, Surpanakha (played by Rakul Preet Singh), becomes infatuated with Rama, setting off a chain of events that leads to her humiliation. Vowing retribution, Ravana steps in to restore his pride, initiating the conflict that leads to Sita’s abduction. Building to a grand finale, the footage showcases high-scale visual effects, mythological weaponry, and massive army battles as Rama vows to defeat Ravana across the three worlds and rescue Sita, signaling the start of the era of Rama. The film is produced by Namit Malhotra’s Prime Focus Studios and Yash’s Monster Mind Creations. Kapoor, Yash, Tiwari and Malhotra, founder of Prime Focus and DNEG CEO, appeared at San Diego Comic-Con to debut the new clip and discuss the making of the epic movies. “Ramayana” Part 1 is set to open during the Diwali holiday frame, with Part 2 following on Diwali 2027. The choice of release window is no accident. Diwali – one of the most widely observed festivals in the Hindu calendar – marks the return of Rama to his kingdom of Ayodhya after 14 years of exile and his victory over Ravana. The lighting of lamps that defines the celebration is said to represent the illumination of Ayodhya on the night its beloved prince came home. Score duties are shared by Oscar-winning composers Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman. DNEG – the eight-time Oscar winning VFX house, whose credits include the “Dune” movies, “Interstellar” and “Inception” – is handling visual effects. Tiwari, whose “Dangal” remains the highest-grossing Indian film ever made, directs from a screenplay by Shridhar Raghavan. Sony Pictures is handling international distribution for all territories outside India and Dharma Productions within India. articles.title: Deadline revealed last week
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Talent Agent Mark Jermin Strongly Refuted Unlawful Activity. A Leaked Contract Raises Questions About His Denial. Paramount Sacrificed Some Cinema History To Win Approval For Its Warner Deal, But Will It Be Enough To Safeguard Europe’s Theatrical Business? Jared Leto Denies Criminal Sexual Conduct: “I Have Never Sexually Assaulted Anyone” View All July 23, 2026 5:09am Mark Jermin Gareth Danks EXCLUSIVE : A prominent British children’s acting agency, which has helped young performers clinch roles in Harry Potter and Hunger Games, could have broken UK agency law by effectively charging actors training fees for the opportunity to secure representation, according to legal experts. In emails seen by Deadline, Mark Jermin Management (MJM) encouraged multiple young people to attend paid-for acting classes, provided by sister company the Mark Jermin Stage School (MJSS), if they wished to be represented by the agency. UK law prohibits entertainment agencies from charging upfront fees for representing their clients. Agencies are only permitted to make money by charging a commission on the fees their clients earn from acting work. Agency law experts said Deadline’s findings raised questions about whether MJM breached these regulations. Related Stories Casting 'Harry Potter' Series Star Ruari Spooner Joins Bill Burr & Chris O'Dowd In Comedy 'Bender' News Lady Gaga Scores Emmy Nomination For "The Dead Dance" From Netflix's 'Wednesday' A spokesperson for MJM founder Mark Jermin strongly denied that representation has “ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services.” Jermin declined to comment on specific examples, with his lawyer stating that it was “impossible” for him to address the allegations because Deadline had refused to hand over copies of the original emails. Deadline did not disclose the original messages for source protection reasons. Watch on Deadline The allegations follow Jermin’s earlier acknowledgment that his company mishandled self-tape auditions, prompted by a Deadline investigation in May . After publication, Jermin described the piece as “deeply unfair,” in part because he said the allegations of audition malpractice were historical and isolated. Since that investigation, Deadline has obtained further evidence of at least two other instances of self-tape audition issues. This includes an incident in January, when a disabled actor felt misled by MJM after being asked to record a self-tape audition and post about it on social media, even though he had not been called to audition by the casting team. Through his attorney, Jermin admitted to mistakes in his company’s dealings with the disabled actor. “We recognise that further concerns and allegations have been raised following recent reporting and we take them extremely seriously,” Jermin’s spokesperson added. “However, we deny unequivocally allegations of deliberate wrongdoing, unlawful conduct or systemic misconduct.” Jermin has engaged an external consultant to review processes at MJM and MJSS with a view to making improvements. Jermin’s lawyer declined to identify the consultancy or its terms of reference. Acting Lessons Linked To Representation Jermin is one of the UK’s best-known children’s agents, unearthing talent including Heartstopper star Kit Connor and Wednesday ’s Evie Templeton, as well as securing roles for actors like Eire Farrell in the Harry Potter series. He has parlayed his expertise into a significant social media presence, which he uses to promote his management work and market acting lessons, promising to make stars out of young people. Jermin’s TikTok updates are a legitimate way to sell services and discover new talent, but behind his popular videos, he has used tactics that have raised questions. Kit Connor in ‘Heartstopper’ Samuel Dore/Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection Deadline has obtained emails and messages spanning a four-year period from January 2021 to October 2025 in which MJM employees, including Jermin himself, told individuals enquiring about representation that the agency prefers to take on new talent through acting classes. UK law generally prohibits agencies like MJM from charging upfront fees and prevents them from making the provision of representation conditional upon the use of other services, such as acting classes. The messages show that MJM repeatedly told students and parents that it “scouts” new clients from lessons. On other occasions, the company was more direct. In one 2023 email, an MJM representative told a parent that the company “only represents” young actors “who regularly train and attend our classes.” Separately, in a 2022 WhatsApp message, Jermin stated that actors “need” to attend a course to be considered for MJM’s new voice work division. Deadline has also received testimony from a dozen current and former Mark Jermin Stage School students/parents, who said it was their understanding that they needed to pay for lessons to be considered for representation. “If you weren’t in the classes, there was no chance you would be signed,” one person alleged. Deadline presented the evidence to three lawyers and two industry experts, all of whom have an understanding of the relevant UK agency law. They said the messages were grounds to suspect that MJM could be in breach of Regulation 5 of the Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003, which states that agencies must not make work-finding services conditional upon work-seekers using other services. The regulations are enforced by the Fair Work Agency, which has the power to inspect agencies. If an agent is found to have flouted the law, they could be fined if they do not put their house in order, though this is rare. The Fair Work Agency declined to comment on MJM, but said it would examine any relevant complaints. “Open & Shut” Case Paul Maynard, a partner in employment law at Gaby Hardwicke Solicitors, said: “On the evidence I have seen, and from Regulation 5, this agency is in breach of the regulations. It seems pretty open and shut, and I can’t see any exemption within the regulations.” In one 2023 message to a parent, MJM explained that having children in classes promotes high standards and allows MJM and MJSS employees to get to know young people before they are put forward for casting opportunities. MJM added that attending lessons is not an “automatic” route to representation as the agency “can’t take on every student.” Similar language is contained in MJSS’s terms and conditions, which state: “Participation in training does not guarantee representation.” Maynard explained: “Regarding language around ‘scouting’ or ‘vetting’ in classes, there’s no wriggle room in Regulation 5 that allows them [MJM] to do it. They’re charging for those classes, and that’s an ancillary service to what they then go and do, which is supply clients for hire and reward.” Seth Roe, a partner at Wiggin, which recently represented casting directory Spotlight in a High Court triumph against Equity in a case relating to agency laws, said: “An agency should not say (or imply) that it will only help a person find work if they also buy an extra service from the agency or from someone connected with the agency. “The reason for the rule is straightforward: access to work should not be used as leverage to pressure actors, performers, models or other work seekers into paying for add-ons they may not need, may not be able to afford, or may feel they have no real choice but to purchase.” He added that a court would likely take a literal interpretation of the regulations, which is to protect work seekers from being exploited. “That could therefore lead to a broad, practical and purposive interpretation, focused on whether a work seeker (or their parents, guardians etc) could reasonably have felt pressured to pay for additional services in order to have a better prospect of securing work,” Roe said. Dugald Johnson, agents’ official at actors’ union Equity, told Deadline: “The law is clear that the only fee an agency may charge a performer is a fee out of earnings from work — commission. Agencies should understand that they cannot make representation conditional upon paying upfront fees, whether for acting classes or any other service. “If members are asked for such fees, Equity advises them not to pay them and to contact the union. It is incumbent on all agencies to engage with and observe basic rules which apply to them, including on fees, not least given the immense trust which performers place in them.” Adrian Marlowe, a Lawspeed attorney who contributed to government thinking when the laws were drafted, said Regulation 5 was engaged because MJM and MJSS are connected and the latter is charging a fee. He added that, although MJM’s emails are not explicitly transactional, they “do indicate that this could be a breach of Regulation 5.” Another industry professional, who has experience in agency laws but did not wish to be named in connection with Jermin, said: “An agency should not require a prospective client to purchase classes, coaching, workshops, photography, or other services as a condition of being considered for representation or for access to employment opportunities.” In a statement, Jermin’s spokesperson said that MJM denies “unequivocally allegations of deliberate wrongdoing, unlawful conduct or systemic misconduct. In particular, we strongly reject any suggestion that representation by Mark Jermin Management has ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services.” Jermin declined to engage with the specific examples presented by Deadline. His lawyer said that it was “impossible” for his client to address the allegations because Deadline had declined to hand over unedited copies of the original emails for source protection reasons. The attorney claimed that a document prepared by Deadline detailing the messages had been edited “significantly,” including quoting extracts “entirely out of context.” Deadline does not accept that any messages were edited to change their meaning. Jermin has also previously “emphatically denied” any unlawful charging. “MJM does not charge, and has never charged, any individual to be managed or represented by it,” his lawyer said in a letter to Deadline in March, adding: “Never has it ever been put to students participating in stage school classes operated by TMJSS that they may be represented by MJM at some point in the future provided that they continue paying to participate in those stage classes.” Self-Tape Mishandling After Deadline published its original investigation into self-tape auditions by Jermin and his companies in May, he posted a statement saying that the allegations regarding the mishandling of self-tapes in 2024 were “historical,” while in correspondence to Deadline through a lawyer, he blamed the issues on administrative staff at his stage school. Deadline has now seen evidence that raises questions about his defense, implicating Jermin in the alleged mishandling of auditions as recently as January. Jermin’s position is that these were isolated mistakes, shorn of context, and were not indicative of “persistent misconduct.” Theatre Royal Bath At the start of 2026, MJM sent an actor an audition for a production of The Secret Garden at The Egg, which is part of the Theatre Royal Bath. Casey, a pseudonym we are using to protect the disabled actor’s identity, believed it to be a legitimate audition. Days earlier, Jermin had told Casey he was pitching him for the role, so when the actor received the audition, he assumed the pitch was successful. Jermin requested that Casey post a social media video thanking MJM for securing him the audition. Casey followed instructions, ending his video by stating: “Thanks so much to the team at Mark Jermin Management for helping to secure me this audition.” After reading Deadline’s story in May, Casey became suspicious about The Secret Garden self-tape and contacted the Theatre Royal Bath. The theater said Casey had not been called to audition and that the casting team had not received his self-tape from MJM. “To find out that something that I put so much effort into was a fabrication was heartbreaking,” Casey told Deadline. He feels misled and exploited, believing he was encouraged to deceive his social media followers. Through his lawyer, Jermin said Casey’s experience was the result of miscommunication at MJM. After talking to Casey about pitching him for the role, Jermin believed a colleague had submitted his audition to the Theatre Royal Bath when, in reality, they had only sent Casey’s acting resume. Jermin’s attorney described it as an “unfortunate error” that he “very much regrets,” but said it was not evidence of “persistent and long-standing wrongdoing regarding the handling of self-tape auditions.” Casey challenged Jermin directly about the self-tape issue over email in May, during which the MJM founder said he had “proof” that the tape was sent. Through his lawyer, he later admitted that this evidence did not exist. Jermin accepted that he should have been more careful in his communication with Casey. Jermin attempted to talk to Casey to explain, but the actor declined. Jermin’s correspondence with the Theatre Royal Bath team also contained misinformation about Casey. He claimed that Casey “sometimes” presents Blue Peter , the iconic BBC kids’ show. Casey has never hosted Blue Peter . Jermin’s spokesperson said: “We understand that some individuals may have had experiences that they were unhappy with and, where mistakes have occurred, we regret any distress caused and remain committed to reviewing and improving our processes. To this end, we have retained the services of an independent consultant who will be reviewing all our processes.” In a second example from January 2023, Jermin emailed an actor we are anonymizing as Max, requesting that he self-tape for a Rice Krispies advert. Jermin copied and pasted a message purporting to be from the casting director. The message contained Max’s full name, suggesting that he was unambiguously the recipient of the audition. When Max requested further information about the role directly from the casting team, he was told that Jermin likely sent the self-tape in “error,” because he had not been called to audition. Jermin’s attorney said his client did not know the identity of Max and was unable to find any record of the audition for the Rice Krispies advert. The lawyer said MJM needed to be provided with copies of all relevant emails and that without them, it was ‘impossible’ to take instructions or to prepare a meaningful response. Deadline declined to do this for source protection reasons. ‘Bridgerton’ Season 3 Netflix The cases follow Deadline’s report in May that revealed MJM sent an actress self-tape auditions for roles in Bridgerton and Coronation Street , but she was later told that she was not called to audition for the series, and her tapes were not received by the casting teams. Jermin said the self-tape issues were due to an administrative error that had since been corrected. In a statement, Jermin’s spokesperson said: “Over more than 30 years, we have supported aspiring performers and their families through an industry that is highly competitive, subjective and often challenging. While individual concerns should always be listened to and considered carefully, we believe it is important that isolated incidents and disputes are viewed fairly and in their proper context. “We remain committed to operating professionally, transparently and in the best interests of those we support. We will continue to listen, learn and strengthen our processes where appropriate, while remaining focused on helping young performers develop and succeed.” If you would like to get in contact with the author of this story, please email jkanter@deadline.com. articles.title: Grammy CEO “Saddened” By BTS Withdrawal, Defends Asian Pop Category: “It’s Never To Divide”
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Ben Affleck Wins ‘Who Wants to Be a Millionaire’ For His Eastern Congo Initiative, Along With Jamie Ding Grammy CEO “Saddened” By BTS Withdrawal, Defends Asian Pop Category: “It’s Never To Divide” Jeff Hiller Got Emmy Nom For 7-Minute ‘Pluribus’ Role Viewers Have Compared To ChatGPT: “I Was Trying To Convey Extreme Love” View All July 29, 2026 5:35pm Grammy CEO responds to BTS's withdrawal from nominations. John Parra/Getty Images for The Recording Academy/Mauro Pimentel/AFP After BTS sent shockwaves through the music industry with their withdrawal from the 69th Grammy Awards , the Recording Academy’s CEO has responded. On Wednesday, shortly after the K-pop removed themselves from consideration in apparent protest over the newly added Best Asian Pop Music Performance category, Grammy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. said he was “saddened” but, “I understand and respect the decision. “I am saddened to hear that BTS has chosen not to participate in the Grammy Awards process this year, but as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision,” he said in a statement. Related Stories News BTS Withdraws From Grammy Consideration In Apparent Protest Over New Asian Pop Category News Grammy Awards Make Changes To Best New Artist Rules & Add Five New Categories “I do want to clarify something that seems to be getting lost in the conversation,” added Mason. “The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists. More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized. It’s never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters.” Watch on Deadline Mason also clarified that submitting music to any genre category does not exclude an artist from submitting to general categories like Record of the Year, Album of the Year and Song of the Year. “Those categories remain open to any eligible recording, regardless of genre. Recognition in a genre category and recognition in the General Field are not mutually exclusive. An artist can absolutely pursue both,” he explained. “The Grammy organization is here to serve music and all the people who make it,” Mason continued. “As we continue to expand the reach, our membership and our awards, regardless of geography or language, I want to emphasize that we will continue to listen to the global music community and work to honor and celebrate all the artists whose music moves the world.” Earlier on Wednesday, BTS members RM, Jin, Suga, J-Hope, Jimin, V and Jungkook posted in a joint statement , “We have decided not to submit for Grammy consideration this year. We hope our music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language. We thank Army and everyone who has always stood by us.” The decision comes after the Recording Academy announced several new categories last month, including the Best Asian Pop Music Performance, which is designed to recognize artistic excellence in “performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets, including but not limited to K-pop, J-pop and C-pop, with meaningful use of one or more Asian languages.” In March, BTS released their 10th studio album Arirang , the group’s first in six years, after pausing to complete their mandator 18-month South Korea military service. articles.title: Paramount Sacrificed Some Cinema History To Win Approval For Its Warner Deal, But Will It Be Enough To Safeguard Europe’s Theatrical Business?
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Paramount Sacrificed Some Cinema History To Win Approval For Its Warner Deal, But Will It Be Enough To Safeguard Europe’s Theatrical Business? Jared Leto Denies Criminal Sexual Conduct: “I Have Never Sexually Assaulted Anyone” ‘Blankety Blank,’ ‘Celebrity Mastermind’ & ‘Live At The Apollo’ All Canceled By The BBC Under Sweeping Content Cuts View All July 30, 2026 12:00am Paramount CEO David Ellison Getty “Cinema may have peaked,” was how United International Pictures sales manager Kenneth Jønsson greeted the arrival of The Odyssey in Norway. “Trust me, this is one for the ages, and a huge reminder of how lucky we are to work with films and filmmakers like this.” Jønsson posted his love letter to Christopher Nolan’s epic on LinkedIn just before the movie’s premiere. A couple of weeks on, there are very real questions about the future of United International Pictures (UIP) and whether it will continue to serve the filmmakers Jønsson admires. That’s because Paramount has agreed to exit UIP, its 50-50 joint venture with Universal Pictures , to secure regulatory approval for its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery in the European Union. In remedies laid down by the European Commission, the EU’s antitrust enforcer, Paramount will need to unwind its links to UIP within 13 months of closing the Warner merger, walking away from a company that has been part of the European cinema landscape for 44 years. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Culture Joyce Carol Oates Defends Christopher Nolan & 'The Odyssey' Against Emily Wilson, Other Critics Books 'The Final Girl Support Group' Heads To Paramount As Film Directed & Adapted By Christopher Landon; Aperture & Muschiettis' Double Dream Producing Paramount declined to comment on how it will disentangle itself from UIP or whether the venture will continue without its stewardship. Universal Pictures also declined to comment on the European Commission ruling last week. UIP did not respond to a request for comment. UIP distributed ‘The Odyssey’ Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal So here’s what we know: Paramount will terminate its 50% stake in UIP, meaning it will have to seek alternative distribution arrangements in the 100 territories in which UIP has a presence. Paramount may be able to tap into Warner Bros. Pictures operations in some of these locations or piggyback on Warner’s existing partnerships, but only if the partner has no role in distributing Universal or Disney films. When Warner had a distribution deal with SF Studios in the Nordics, for example, if Paramount had wanted to switch its UIP films into this agreement, it would have needed to establish that SF Studios had no similar arrangements with Universal and Disney. This would ensure Paramount does not fall foul of European Commission conditions. Whatever the outcome, UIP will have significantly fewer titles to handle, which will inevitably create uncertainty for the company’s 200 employees (even if it does distribute some non-Paramount-Universal titles, such as Lionsgate’s Michael ). Headquartered in Chiswick, a leafy suburb of west London, UIP does not have a CEO, though former STX Entertainment executive Rhiannon Harries serves as chief operating officer and appears to be one of the company’s most senior figures. Paramount and Universal lawyers act as directors of UIP’s British operations. UIP posted sales of nearly £198M ($263M) in 2024, per its most recent accounts filed at the UK’s Companies House. It recorded a pre-tax profit of £12.2M. In its pomp, UIP boasted box office takings of $2.5 billion, but was much diminished in 2007, when Paramount and Universal took direct control of distribution in key markets, including France, Brazil, and Italy. Stewart Till, the British executive who ran UIP for four years until 2006, said Paramount’s exit would be the end of an era for a company that combined the “best of Hollywood with local decision makers.” He said the exit was “not irrelevant” for Paramount given that it will have to make alternative arrangements in UIP territories. “It’s not a coincidence that Paramount hasn’t done that since 2007,” he said. There is a feeling, however, that divesting from UIP is a small concession for Paramount to make in the context of an industry-reshaping $111B union with Warner Bros. A well-placed industry executive said: “I can’t see it making any difference, to be honest. The pieces will just move around between even fewer players, meaning even less competition. Maybe there needs to be further regulation introduced so that no single local distribution company has dominant market share, and other ways to stimulate competition and innovation.” The International Union of Cinemas (UNIC), which represents cinema operators across 39 European territories, agrees. Laura Houlgatte, UNIC’s chief executive, told Deadline: “While the remedy addresses an important structural issue, it does not tackle similar risks that arise from theatrical distribution arrangements outside the UIP territories, nor does the Commission decision address a number of wider concerns that UNIC raised throughout the review.” UIP re-released ‘Top Gun’ and ‘Top Gun: Maverick’ in cinemas earlier this year Paramount During the European Commission’s investigation process, Houlgatte said the UNIC advocated for “safeguards around theatrical exclusivity and release windows, as well as measures to help maintain a strong and diverse pipeline of films for cinemas and audiences.” Paramount CEO David Ellison has attempted to assuage these concerns with commitments to release more than 30 cinema films a year and hold to a minimum theatrical window of 45 days. He will continue making this case while the merger is on ice as Paramount fights a lawsuit from 12 U.S. state attorneys general, who argue the deal stifles competition for theatrical film distribution. The Balanced Economy Project, an apolitical UK non-profit that lobbies against monopolies, is not convinced. It said the European Commission’s UIP remedy “does nothing obvious about the future bargaining power of a combined Paramount-Warner studio.” The Balanced Economy Project added: “Cinemas would still face one fewer independent major studio. Broadcasters and platforms would still face a larger owner of premium rights. Producers and creative suppliers would still face another reduction in major routes to market.” Paramount breaking bonds with Universal signals the end of some European cinema history, but discovering whether it’s enough to safeguard a precarious business from a new monolith will be its own odyssey of sorts. articles.title: ‘This Is Birmingham’: TV Series Adaptation Of Surprise Prime Video UK Hit In Works
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Claire Foy & Matthew Macfadyen To Lead David Nicholls Novel Adaptation ‘You Are Here’ For BBC & Starz ‘This Is Birmingham’: TV Series Adaptation Of Surprise Prime Video UK Hit In Works Disney+ Korea’s Record-Setting Supernatural Reality Show ‘Battle Of Fates’ Getting Spin-Off View All July 30, 2026 12:06am 'This is Birmingham' became a surprise hit on Prime Video UK Courtesy EXCLUSIVE: It’s the surprise Prime Video UK action breakout of the year, and now This is Birmingham is getting a TV series adaptation. The pic, made with a minimal budget, peaked at number five on Prime Video UK’s top ten films earlier this week, and creator Kay S. Ubhi told Deadline a TV series adaptation is now in development. The film, which Ubhi wrote and stars in, is billed as a “visceral crime drama” set in the depths of the UK’s brutal underworld. It follows AK (Ubhi), the inexperienced but ambitious son of a recently imprisoned Birmingham crime boss (Navdeep Monga), who steps up to lead the family business, only to be met by rival gangs determined to take over. The pic also stars the likes of Jerome Richards, Jag Patel and Wayne Nelson. Related Stories Casting Jay Baruchel, Kevin Durand, Amanda Ip & Ciara Bravo Join 'Reacher' For Season 5 News Crunchyroll And Starz Launch Bundle On Prime Video Michael L. Cowan, the UK film sales and production veteran, was among the producers of the indie pic and is also attached to the TV adaptation, Ubhi told Deadline in an interview today. Watch on Deadline “The TV series is currently in development,” he said. “It expands the world of This is Birmingham into a bigger, character-driven crime drama. We’re developing it with Bafta winner Michael L. Cowan, and the next step is bringing together the right production partners to take it into production.” Ubhi, who self-funded This is Birmingham , said his film had resonated with audiences, stacking up against Hollywood movies in the Prime Video charts, thanks to a “real audience for authentic British crime dramas” and was now being distributed in the U.S. on transactional on-demand platforms. He also pointed to the hot streak Birmingham, which is often referred to as England’s second city, has been on through the likes of Peaky Blinders and This Town . “The film offers a fresh unique perspective through its characters, emotional story and, of course, the Birmingham theme,” said Ubhi. “Birmingham already has a lot of intrigue because of its reputation and shows like Peaky Blinders .” As for funding the pic himself, “It was a huge personal commitment over several years, but I really believed in the story. I wanted to prove that it can be done even in the most unconventional ways.” As of press time, This is Birmingham is sitting at number ten in the most-watched action movies on Prime Video UK. articles.title: Claire Foy & Matthew Macfadyen To Lead David Nicholls Novel Adaptation ‘You Are Here’ For BBC & Starz
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Claire Foy & Matthew Macfadyen To Lead David Nicholls Novel Adaptation ‘You Are Here’ For BBC & Starz ‘This Is Birmingham’: TV Series Adaptation Of Surprise Prime Video UK Hit In Works Disney+ Korea’s Record-Setting Supernatural Reality Show ‘Battle Of Fates’ Getting Spin-Off View All July 30, 2026 1:00am Claire Foy and Matthew Macfadyen Juankr, Josh Wool Matthew Macfadyen ( Succession ) and Claire Foy ( All of Us Strangers ) will star in You Are Here , a BBC and Starz adaptation of author David Nicholls ‘ bestseller of the same name. Nicholls has penned the eight-part adaptation, which will be produced by Normal People maker Element Pictures . Lenny Abrahamson , who directed Normal People , is the director. Element parent Fremantle has international sales rights, with De Maio Entertainment overseeing the partnership with Starz, which has greenlit the show alongside the BBC. Set along the coast-to-coast walking trail from the Lake District to Robin Hood’s Bay in North Yorkshire in England, You Are Here ” will be filmed in the Lake District and around Manchester. Related Stories News Gregg Araki Reveals 'Now Apocalypse' Season 2 Was Written For Starz, Mirrored Show's Cancellation: "So Prophetic" News Jared Leto Denies Criminal Sexual Conduct: "I Have Never Sexually Assaulted Anyone" Macfadyen and Foy lead the cast as Michael and Marnie, respectively. Per the synopsis, “When a mutual friend throws them together, Marnie and Michael unexpectedly find themselves setting off on an epic walk. Against the odds, they end up on the brink of a relationship that neither was looking for, but which might be exactly the one they both need.” Watch on Deadline “I’m so delighted to be working on You Are Here with Element, the BBC, Starz and Lenny, whose work I’ve admired for many years,” said Nicholls, the prolific author whose book One Day was adapted as a romantic drama for Netflix in 2024. “Matthew and Claire are both just dream casting, wonderful in comedy and drama, so detailed and thoughtful and sympathetic,” he added. “The intention with the novel was to write a close-up study of a relationship, but set against this magnificent landscape, and that’s our ambition here too; to make something both intimate and epic, funny and dramatic, a romantic comedy with real emotion. We can’t wait to bring Marnie and Michael’s journey to the screen.” Abrahamson called the novel “such a beautiful love story – funny, profound and ultimately deeply hopeful,” while Element co-founder and executive producer Ed Guiney praised Abrahamson and Nicholls as “two of the most talented creators working today.” Nicholls Abrahamson are executive producers alongside Foy and MacFadyen, Guiney, Andrew Lowe and Emma Norton for Element Pictures and Jonny Richards and Anna Ferguson for the BBC. The series is produced by Clare Shepherd. Lindsay Salt, BBC Director of Drama, said: “Like countless others, I loved this book, packed full of charm, humor, heartache and joy. The combination of David’s wonderful scripts, Lenny back directing on the BBC, Element Pictures producing, and Claire and Mathew leading our cast is a real gift. I can’t wait for Marnie and Michael to spring off the page and onto the screen. BBC viewers are in for a treat.” You Are Here comes soon after Starz boarded another British drama, the Bella Ramsey-led Channel 4 show Maya . Over recent months, it has also acquired has acquired the BBC’s Rebecca Hall-fronted The Listeners , Sky’s Amadeus and Channel 4’s Russell T. Davies-created Alan Cumming-led drama Tip Toe . Kathryn Busby, President of Original Programming, Starz, said: “ You Are Here is disarming, sly and deeply romantic. It captures something true and aching about the way we love now. Together with our partners at the BBC, we are thrilled to be working with the dream team of David, Lenny, Claire, Matthew and Element Pictures to bring this beautiful love story to life. It’s a perfect fit for our Starz audience.” Foy is repped by Independent Talent, UTA and Tapestry, and Macfadyen by UTA and Hamilton Hodell. articles.title: Neil Reading Dies: Top UK Entertainment PR Whose Client List Included John Cleese & Lenny Henry Was 56
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Neil Reading Dies: Top UK Entertainment PR Whose Client List Included John Cleese & Lenny Henry Was 56 A24 Options ‘HappyHead’ Author Josh Silver’s Debut Adult Novel ‘Fruit Fly’ For TV ‘Assassin’s Creed’ Star Laura Marcus Behind Channel 4 Comedy ‘F**k Ups’ View All July 30, 2026 1:39am Neil Reading (left) Dave Benett/Getty Images for Mandarin Oriental Hyde Park Neil Reading , UK publicist to the likes of John Cleese and Dawn French, has died aged 56. According to The Sun, which carried a number of tributes, the PR guru died following a short illness. Reading ran a PR firm, Neil Reading PR, and was an extremely well-known publicist in the UK entertainment world. He launched his agency in 1992 and specialized in entertainment along with lifestyle PR. Reading’s clients included Monty Python co-creator Cleese, Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power star Lenny Henry, British comic French, comedian Jason Manford and another beloved comic, the late Victoria Wood. French told The Sun: “Neil Reading was a one-off, such a kind, decent, intelligent man, a proper gentleman in the old-fashioned way, quietly magnificent. Our work relationship became a very real and trusting friendship. He has been my ally and fierce protector through so much and for so long. I don’t quite know how I’ll manage without him. Sleep tight darlin’ heart.” Watch on Deadline Manford added: “Describing Neil as my PR manager does not come close to describing what he meant to me. He was a trusted friend of almost 20 years, a confidant and one of the most loyal, noble and brilliant men I have ever known.” Reading is survived by his wife Claire and daughter Rosa. Projects from Central and South Asia also stand out with new works from Kyrgyzstan’s Dastan Zhapar Ryskeldi; Sri Lanka’s Prasanna Vithanage, who won the Jiseok Award in 2023 for Paradise ; Pakistan’s Eshah Shakeeland; and India’s Dominic Sangma, Tribeny Rai Stenzin Tankyong and Payal Sethi ( see full list of projects below ). Jared Leto Denies Criminal Sexual Conduct: “I Have Never Sexually Assaulted Anyone” View All July 30, 2026 3:01am Mark Jermin Management is one of the UK's best-known children’s agents Keagan Henman/Unsplash EXCLUSIVE : Mark Jermin Management, the prominent UK children’s agency, has stripped a clause from some actor contracts that made it “conditional” for clients to train at its sister stage school, potentially breaching UK law. Deadline revealed last week that Mark Jermin Management (MJM), which discovered stars including Heartstopper lead Kit Connor and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms breakout Dexter Sol Ansell , could have broken UK agency regulations by effectively charging actors training fees for the opportunity to secure representation. In emails seen by Deadline, MJM encouraged young people to attend paid-for acting classes, provided by sister company the Mark Jermin Stage School (MJSS), if they wished to be represented by the agency. In one 2023 email, an MJM representative told a parent that the company “only represents” young actors “who regularly train and attend our classes.” UK law prohibits agencies from charging upfront fees for representing their clients. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Mark Jermin, TikTok-Famous Agent Who Discovered 'Harry Potter' & 'Wednesday' Stars, May Have Broken UK Agency Law News Everything We Know About The 'Heartstopper' Movie So Far In a statement last week, a spokesperson for MJM founder Mark Jermin strongly denied that representation has “ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services.” Following publication, Deadline obtained a leaked copy of a 2025 MJM representation contract, which raised serious questions about the accuracy of the agency’s statement. The fourth paragraph of the leaked contract reads: “If you have been scouted from Mark Jermin classes or events, this is a conditional offer given with the understanding that you will continue training with Mark Jermin so the agency can monitor your progress and development. You agree to disclose any intention to leave training and discuss this with the agency ahead of any action.” Section of leaked Mark Jermin Management contract Deadline confronted MJM with the contract clause and asked how it was compatible with last week’s statement. A spokesperson said the clause only appeared in a small number of client contracts and was a “recommendation” that was never enforced. The MJM spokesperson added that the clause would be stripped from agreements as part of an ongoing review by an external consultant. Deadline presented the clause to three agency law experts, all of whom said it raised questions about MJM’s denials of unlawful conduct. Adrian Marlowe, a Lawspeed attorney who specializes in agency laws, said it was a “clear breach” of Regulation 5 of the UK Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003, which states that agencies must not make work-finding services conditional upon work-seekers using other services. “Use of phrases such as ‘with the understanding that,’ and ‘so the agency can monitor’ cannot alter the clear condition which comes into effect when the offer is accepted,” he explained. An MJM spokesperson said: “The wording you have identified is confined to a very small number of contracts in our overall database. The majority of clients of both the stage school and MJM do not have this wording in their contracts and, as part of our ongoing work with business consultants, the wording has been removed from all contracts. “The reason for the wording was to enable the team at MJM and the stage school to monitor and assess the actors’ progress in order to gauge their ability and suitability for any roles that they might be put forward for. “In this sense it’s more of a recommendation and the condition was never enforced. No payment was demanded upfront and clients were free to end their association with the stage school while continuing to be represented by MJM without prejudice. A number of clients have opted to discontinue their training and are still represented by MJM.” The source who shared the contract with Deadline said: “These words in the contract were not seen as a ‘recommendation’ … it was seen as ‘conditional,’ as per the wording in the contract.” They added: “These two words have very different meanings.” In a statement last week, Jermin’s spokesperson said that MJM denies “unequivocally allegations of deliberate wrongdoing, unlawful conduct or systemic misconduct. In particular, we strongly reject any suggestion that representation by Mark Jermin Management has ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services.” Jermin is one of the UK’s best-known children’s agents, unearthing talent including Wednesday’s Evie Templeton, Harry Potter series star Eire Farrell, and Iona Bell, who will feature in Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping . He has parlayed his expertise into a significant social media presence, which he uses to promote his management work and market acting lessons, promising to make stars out of young people. articles.title: San Sebastian Sets 2026 New Directors Lineup
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘Welcome II The Terrordome’ Returns To Cinemas With New Restoration, Ngozi Onwurah Discusses How The Film Was Almost Lost & Plans For Her Next Project ‘Elsinore’ Starring Andrew Scott & Olivia Colman To Open London Film Festival Glen Hansard Dies: Oscar-Winning ‘Once’ Songwriter, Actor & Musician Was 56 View All July 30, 2026 3:53am Billy Lumby's 'Florid' © Florid Limited, British Broadcasting Corporation & Film I Väst 2026. The San Sebastian Film Festival has confirmed the lineup of filmmakers that will participate in the New Directors programme at this year’s festival, which is set to run from September 18 to 26. Scroll down for the full lineup. Filmmakers from Bulgaria, Chile, Germany, Iran, Japan, Kazakhstan, Mexico, Norway, South Korea, Spain, Taiwan, the UK and Ukraine will present their first and second feature films in the New Directors sidebar. The Bad Son (El mal hijo), the debut feature by Jaime Lorente, will open the sidebar. The film’s official synopsis reads: When 11-year-old Ruben’s father mysteriously disappears, the boy has to move in with his grandmother, a woman he barely knows. In a rural setting where time seems to have stood still, the child will learn that family wounds are passed down from one generation to another, and will try to find a way to heal them as he grows. ​ Related Stories Festivals Marion Cotillard New Image & First Sales Unveiled For Nicole Garcia's San Sebastian-Bound 'Milo' News Mike Leigh's 'Tender Loving Care' & Pablo Larraín Series 'My Sad Dead' Among Titles Added To San Sebastian Lineup New Directors will close with Billy Lumby’s debut film Florid . The film follows a young man who struggles to balance his mental problems, medication, and drugs with his musical ambitions. The official synopsis reads: Jamal, who has a diagnosis of schizophrenia, lives in a supported housing block, alongside other people with mental health issues. Frustrated by the side effects of his medication, he stops taking it, making the voices he hears become more frequent and extreme. Increasingly changeable in mood, Jamal builds a friendship with Kyla, another resident. But as the voices become more intense, Jamal must confront the blurred line between reality and past family events to come to terms with his voices. Watch on Deadline San Sebastian announced further titles from its official competition earlier this week. Titles set for the Spanish fest include Mike Leigh’s latest feature Tender Loving Care and My Sad Dead , a new series from Chilean filmmaker Pablo Larraín. My Sad Dead will screen at San Sebastian in its feature-length format. Starring are Mercedes Morán, Dolores Fonzi, and Carolina Álvarez. The project is based on four short stories by Mariana Enríquez, and tells the story of Ema, a woman with the ability to see and hear the dead. Leigh’s Tender Loving Care will arrive at San Sebastian after a showing at TIFF. Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson, Kate O’Flynn, and Alice Bailey Johnson star in the film. No synopsis for Tender Loving Care has been provided on either the San Sebastian or TIFF website. San Sebastian simply describes the film as an “insightful exploration of the contemporary world.” The 2026 New Directors Lineup: El mal hijo / The Bad Son Jaime Lorente (Spain) Country(ies) of production: Spain. Cast: Miguel Ángel Puro, Susi Sanchéz, Hugo Arbués, Óscar de la Fuente, Abel de la Fuente Opening Film When 11-year-old Ruben’s father mysteriously disappears, the boy has to move in with his grandmother, a woman he barely knows. In a rural setting where time seems to have stood still, the child will learn that family wounds are passed down from one generation to another, and will try to find a way to heal them as he grows. ​ Florid Billy Lumby (United Kingdom) Country(ies) of production: United Kingdom – Sweden. Cast: Jonathan Jules, Saskia Chana, Unknown T Closing Film Jamal, who has a diagnosis of schizophrenia, lives in a supported housing block, alongside other people with mental health issues. Frustrated by the side effects of his medication, he stops taking it, making the voices he hears become more frequent and extreme. Increasingly changeable in mood, Jamal builds a friendship with Kyla, another resident. But as the voices become more intense, Jamal must confront the blurred line between reality, and past family events, to come to terms with his voices. Bloques erráticos / Erratics Thomas Woodroffe (Chile) Country(ies) of production: Chile – France – Argentina. Cast: Denis Lavant, Daniel Muñoz Freeing himself after spending a hundred years trapped in a glacier, the ghost of the filmmaker Lucien Castelnau wanders through a futuristic Patagonia, where technological progress clashes with forgotten stories. Unable to rest while his cinematic legacy remains unseen, he crosses a world that has deleted him from its memory, in search of a place in history and of spectators, who can finally bring his lost work back to life. Body of Glass Naëmi Ada (Germany) Country(ies) of production: Germany – France. Cast: Soma Pysall, Elise Tilloloy, Manuel Severin, Younès Boucif After a violent incident with her controlling partner Felix, dancer Tian flees their shared life in Marseille. Isolated and desperate for connection, she infiltrates the grieving circle of a young man she never knew. But as she becomes entangled in their mourning and affection, she hides a dangerous secret at home. When lies, grief and reality collapse into each other, Tian must choose whether to break the cycle. Cute Marlene Emilie Lyngstad (Norway) Country(ies) of production: Denmark – Sweden – Norway. Cast: Jan Gunnar Røise, Gina Jaqueline , Karin Bertling, Kitt Maiken Mortensen, Molly Kirk Rasmussen Troubled by forbidden feelings for his seven-year-old stepdaughter, Richard decides to leave his girlfriend. He retreats to his childhood home to renovate ahead of its sale, but his self-imposed exile is disrupted by the childlike presence of his mother’s caregiver, Stella. He soon discovers her double life as a Lolita camgirl, and the two develop a transgressive surrogate father-daughter relationship. Their constructed reality begins to unravel when the stepdaughter he left behind reaches out. Esta soledad / This Solitude Javier Giner (Spain) Country(ies) of production: Spain. Cast: Oriol Pla, Marina Salas, Gemma Martínez, Kai Etxaniz, Itziar Lazkano Leo and Lorea have loved one another. Maybe they still do. But something in them has broken. After five years, their relationship is done. He looks after his sick father, trapped between responsibility and an emotional void that weighs him down. She, caught up in poorly-paid jobs and personal crises, tries to get her life back on track without really knowing where to begin. They are two bodies, tired and alone, pierced by their precarious situation, by unresolved issues, by the emotional legacy of a generation who always seem to come late to everything: to love, to stability, to maturity, to serenity, to personal satisfaction. ​ Lovers Sleep Alone Massih Parsaei (Iran) Country(ies) of production: Germany. Cast: Pooyesh Frozandeh, Ava Darvishi, Marcel Kohler, Wolfgang Wobéto WIP Europa 2025 Iman has built his life in Berlin around absence. From his family, from Iran, from being known. He fills the silence with work, invented stories, and nights with a man he meets for sex in the park. When his cousin, whom he barely knows, arrives from Tehran for a brief visit, what he left behind quietly finds its way back to him. Morro Rodrigo García Saiz (Mexico) Country(ies) of production: Mexico . Cast: Gustavo Sánchez Parra, Anna Diaz, Ernesto Meléndez Mateo is a small-town vet. Since his son died, he has lived a life of silent routines and nameless guilt. The violence of the place isn’t immediately visible: it sits there, lurking, like a never-ending echo. This fragile balance is broken when Mateo has to heal Morro, the local capo’s injured dog. The animal’s everyday care leads to an unexpected bond: a relationship with neither judgement nor words, that enables Mateo to recover the meaning of life. Mugalim Ayana Nurdinova (Kazakhstan) Country(ies) of production: Kazakhstan. Cast: Oljas Dalelkhan, Rustem Zhanyamanov, Shynar Janysbekova, Olga Landina, Gulnara Dusmatova, Akif Petrov, Madina Yesmanova, Anna Starchenko, Ruslan Duysembekov Zhandos, a music teacher, lives in the small town of Balkhash and dreams of moving to a big city. He is loved by his students, and the school turns a blind eye to his side jobs. When a patron nostalgic for his hometown arrives, Zhandos is given a chance to leave. He must decide what matters more: the art within him, or himself within art. Obuvkite na bashta mi / My Father’s Shoes Hristo Simeonov (Bulgaria) Country(ies) of production: Bulgaria – France. Cast: Valeria Varbanova, Tanya Shahova, Vyara Kolarova Mima has grown up in the shadow of her father’s absence, raised by her uncompromising mother, Boyka. When news of his death arrives, and his body returns to their village, recognition becomes both duty and dilemma. As Boyka refuses to face the man she once loved, mother and daughter confront a silent past, forcing Mima to decide what it means to inherit a life she never chose. Ri Guang / Will You Still Be My Friend Lu Po-Shun (Taiwan) Country(ies) of production: Taiwan – Singapore. Cast: Jaden Wang, Aloysius Looi, Lung Tien Hsiang, Lu Yi-Ching, Andie Chen, Kate Pang Amid an escalating feud in a rural Taiwanese village, a boy struggles to protect his secret friendship with his Singapore-raised best friend as adult conflicts threaten to tear them apart, while he quietly begins to question the true nature of his feelings for his friend. Sieben Tage Februar / February, Seven Days Tatjana Moutchnik (Ukraine) Country(ies) of production: Germany – Austria – Spain. Cast: Serhii Korshykov, Volodymyr Holosniak, Maria Shtofa, Arsenii Markov, Moisej Bazijan, Daria Guitbout WIP Europa 2025 Two different notions of family identity clash when a man from Odesa and his son visit his brother in Germany for the funeral of their mother, the day before the Ukraine war breaks out. The Ballet Lesson Kazuya Murayama (Japan) Country(ies) of production: Japan. Cast: Vadim Bushmakin, Nikita Kondo, Niina Kondo, Yukina Shimizu In a provincial Japanese town, Japanese-Russian siblings Nikita and Nina live an isolated life with their Russian grandparents, knowing their absent parents only through stories. When their father Nikolai suddenly returns, he takes them on a journey to see their mother Yuki, a Japanese ballet dancer. Along the way, the children discover unfamiliar landscapes, brief encounters, and the fragile bonds of family. The World Before Yoon Dan-bi (South Korea) Country(ies) of production: South Korea – Japan – France. Cast: Su-bin Sim, Eo-jin Kim Seventeen-year-old Jin has never left the island where she was born—a place with no road to the mainland, where the sea quietly sets the rhythm of everyday life. When Dujae returns for his grandmother’s funeral, he stays alone in the house she left behind. Jin begins finding small excuses to visit him, and little by little, seeing him becomes part of her everyday life. As summer wears on, the island she has always known begins to feel unfamiliar—the roads, the sea, the faces around her, all subtly transformed. Jin finds herself looking at it, and at herself, for the first time. But summer, like everything else on the island, will not stay.
